headline: KP police get tech to monitor counterterrorism operations
description: Drones, anti-drone systems integrated into Peshawar’s Safe City network.
author: Umer Farooq
article_text:
PESHAWAR: The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police have integrated anti-drone systems and surveillance drones operating across the province into the Safe City Peshawar’s Command and Control Centre to strengthen security and surveillance capabilities.

With the integration of Safe City cameras and anti-drone systems, live video and surveillance feeds from police drones operating anywhere in the province, including during field operations and offensives carried out against terrorists by the police and the Counter Terrorism Department (CTD), can now be monitored at the Command and Control Centre.

Under the new system, hostile quadcopters and drones will not only be detected promptly but also neutralised, KP Safe Cities Project Director Deputy Inspector General Ijaz Ahmad said.

Addressing a news conference at the Command and Control Centre, DIG Ahmad said anti-drone systems installed in Peshawar and other cities had been linked to the centre.

Drones, anti-drone systems integrated into Peshawar’s Safe City network

He said live monitoring of police operations, including those conducted by the CTD across the province, had also become possible, facilitating the timely sharing of information.

The DIG said modern anti-drone systems had already been deployed in Peshawar, Dera Ismail Khan, Lakki Marwat, Tank and Bannu districts to meet evolving security requirements and counter emerging warfare threats. Anti-drone guns had also been provided to police personnel in remote and sensitive areas of the province, he added.

He said the objective was to enhance the police’s ability to promptly detect and neutralise potential threats posed by hostile quadcopters and drones.

The DIG said monitoring and control of police surveillance drones across the province had also been incorporated into the central system.

“Now, during a police operation in any area, live video footage captured by drones will be transmitted to the central Command and Control Centre. This will keep senior police officers directly informed about the ground situation and help them support field operations effectively,” he said.

However, he said the lack of internet connectivity in some areas remained a challenge. Steps were being taken in collaboration with the Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco) to address the issue, he added.

He said the integrated use of modern technology, drone surveillance, anti-drone systems and centralised monitoring would further strengthen the police’s operational capabilities, security surveillance and response to militant threats.

Making the policing system more effective, coordinated and modern through technology was the need of the hour, he said, adding that the Safe Cities project was providing technical support to the KP police in this regard.

Meanwhile, the KP police have established a specialised human resource division trained in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) combat to wage high-tech warfare against terrorists, whose use of drones is evolving from surveillance and ammunition drops to swarm attacks.

The UAV division, initially conceived as an idea, was established in response to advances in terrorists’ capabilities and their growing shift from conventional street fighting to aerial warfare.

The personnel have been trained in modern drone operation, aerial surveillance, intelligence gathering, counterterrorism, protection of sensitive installations and the use of UAV technology in high-risk operations.

The division is the first of its kind established by a police department in the country.

An official said the KP police had realised that technology alone was insufficient and had taken the crucial step of establishing a specialised division of personnel trained in UAV operations.

“These personnel are not only trained to operate drones for surveillance but are also capable of conducting electronic warfare against hostile UAVs,” he added.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: Saudi-led coalition says it downs drone over oil-rich Eastern Region
description: The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said that it intercepted and destroyed a drone over Saudi Arabia’s...
article_text:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said that it intercepted and destroyed a drone over Saudi Arabia’s oil-rich Eastern Region as attacks by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis group continue, AFP reports.

Cross-border fighting involving the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa, has intensified amid the US-Israeli war on Iran, opening another front in the conflict.

headline: Qatari delegation arrives in Tehran for peace talks
description: Oman rescues 25 sailors after merchant ship attacked, set ablaze; Iran halts three oil tankers in Hormuz for "unauthorised crossing".
author: Agencies
article_text:
• Oman rescues 25 sailors after merchant ship attacked, set ablaze• Iran halts three oil tankers in Hormuz for ‘unauthorised crossing’• G20 talks overshadowed by deep rifts over conflicts in Iran, Ukraine

TEHRAN: A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with senior Iranian officials, state media reported, as mediators press efforts to revive peace talks with the United States amid rising fears of a return to hostilities in the Middle East war.

The delegation, led by a senior adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, came to discuss “bilateral relations … as well as regional developments”, the state news agency IRNA said.

It is the latest in a string of visits by senior officials from several countries to the Iranian capital in recent days, as fears grow that the war, now in its eighth month, could flare up again.

Qatar and Pakistan have mediated talks since an April ceasefire. The war began on Feb 28, when US-Israeli strikes on Iran killed the former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Iran retaliated with attacks on Israel and US assets, and has since blocked ships from using the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil consumption.

The tension at sea was underlined on Friday when Oman said it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship that was targeted and set ablaze.

Muscat’s navy carried out an evacuation of the crew of the Panama-flagged RITI after a fire broke out on board, Oman’s Maritime Security Centre said.

Separately, Iran said three oil tankers had been halted as they crossed the blockaded strait. The Revolutionary Guards said two vessels attempting to pass through an unauthorised route “encountered incidents and were brought to a halt” in waters south of the strait after ignoring radio warnings.

A third supertanker, carrying two million barrels of oil, exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine while on an unauthorised route, the Guards added.

Meanwhile, the fallout from the conflict has reached the diplomatic stage in the United States. Speaking to G20 counterparts in Atlanta, including Russia’s Sergei Lavrov, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the world faced a critical “moment of choosing” in tackling “interconnected economic and geopolitical crises” as the wars in Ukraine and Iran deepen divisions among members.

The strains were visible before the two-day meeting began. A traditional group photograph was cancelled after European officials objected to appearing alongside Lavrov.

The German foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said: “There is no normality with Russia.”

Experts and diplomats said the deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East were likely to derail any unified action or joint statement.

The gathering, held just days before the US midterm elections, also comes as global energy prices have soared since the US war on Iran began. It sets the stage for a G20 leaders’ summit in December at Donald Trump’s Doral resort in Miami.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

The delegation, led by a senior adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, came to discuss “bilateral relations … as well as regional developments”, the state news agency IRNA said.

It is the latest in a string of visits by senior officials from several countries to the Iranian capital in recent days, as fears grow that the war, now in its eighth month, could flare up again.

Qatar and Pakistan have mediated talks since an April ceasefire. The war began on Feb 28, when US-Israeli strikes on Iran killed the former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

Iran retaliated with attacks on Israel and US assets, and has since blocked ships from using the Strait of Hormuz, which normally carries about a fifth of global oil consumption.

The tension at sea was underlined on Friday when Oman said it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship that was targeted and set ablaze.

Muscat’s navy carried out an evacuation of the crew of the Panama-flagged RITI after a fire broke out on board, Oman’s Maritime Security Centre said.

Separately, Iran said three oil tankers had been halted as they crossed the blockaded strait. The Revolutionary Guards said two vessels attempting to pass through an unauthorised route “encountered incidents and were brought to a halt” in waters south of the strait after ignoring radio warnings.

A third supertanker, carrying two million barrels of oil, exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine while on an unauthorised route, the Guards added.

Meanwhile, the fallout from the conflict has reached the diplomatic stage in the United States. Speaking to G20 counterparts in Atlanta, including Russia’s Sergei Lavrov, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the world faced a critical “moment of choosing” in tackling “interconnected economic and geopolitical crises” as the wars in Ukraine and Iran deepen divisions among members.

The strains were visible before the two-day meeting began. A traditional group photograph was cancelled after European officials objected to appearing alongside Lavrov.

The German foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, said: “There is no normality with Russia.”

Experts and diplomats said the deep rifts over the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East were likely to derail any unified action or joint statement.

The gathering, held just days before the US midterm elections, also comes as global energy prices have soared since the US war on Iran began. It sets the stage for a G20 leaders’ summit in December at Donald Trump’s Doral resort in Miami.

headline: Barbs fly in Senate over rising poverty, PTI women’s detention
description: Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas questions why elderly women were being detained under the Maintenance of Public Order.
author: Iftikhar A. Khan
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: The Senate on Friday witnessed heated exchanges over rising poverty, the health and detention of PTI women leaders and activists, including Noreen Niazi, and an alleged increase in extrajudicial killings reaching Islamabad.

PTI parliamentary leader Senator Ali Zafar cited a World Bank report in the House, saying 48 per cent of people living below the poverty line in the region were in Pakistan.

“According to the poverty index, those earning less than three dollars are below the poverty line,” he said. “This is a failure of our government. Inflation has increased and its impact is reaching the poor.”

He said many areas lacked drinking water, while secondary schools were unavailable in several places. “Instead of focusing on these things, we are imposing governor’s rule and emergency,” he said, referring to the political situation in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

PTI senators demand proper treatment, family access for Noreen Niazi

PTI Senator Mohsin Aziz protested over the treatment of Noreen Niazi, a sister of PTI founder Imran Khan. “Why is so much cruelty being done to Noreen Niazi? She is a 70-year-old ailing woman. She should be given treatment and her family should be allowed to meet her,” he said.

The Minister of State for Interior, Tallal Chaudhry, assured the House that there would be no negligence regarding her health.

“She was brought to hospital not on her wish but on doctors’ advice. Treatment is not done on wish, treatment is done on doctors’ advice. Doctors will decide where to take her,” he said.

“As she is a woman, we are more sensitive in this regard. It is the responsibility of the government,” he added.

PTI Senator Azam Swati said he had spoken to Ms Niazi’s husband, who informed him that her treatment was progressing well.

“He thanked the government for allowing her to meet her elder daughter. This is a good step by the government,” Mr Swati said.

The minister’s remarks that treatment would be determined by doctors rather than Ms Niazi’s wishes triggered protests and sloganeering by PTI members.

“Let the House run, it will not work like this,” PPP Senator Shahadat Awan, who was presiding over the session, intervened.

Senate Opposition Leader Allama Raja Nasir Abbas welcomed the decision to allow Ms Niazi to meet her daughter, but criticised the detention of PTI women leaders and activists.

He referred to Dr Yasmin Rashid and Imran Khan’s sisters, questioning why elderly women were being detained under the Maintenance of Public Order (MPO).

“Women must be respected, but here they have been put in jails. They can also be kept under house arrest,” he said.

He warned that such treatment would damage the government’s reputation and demanded the release of women detainees.

Mr Abbas also criticised the imposition of governor’s rule in KP, accusing the government of taking control of the province and restricting political activity.

He said economic progress required the rule of law and urged the government to focus on hunger, poverty and public welfare rather than detaining political opponents and their relatives. “Release our sisters and daughters from jails now,” he demanded.

Meanwhile, JUI-F Senator Kamran Murtaza expressed concern over a rise in extrajudicial killings over the past few days, warning that such incidents had now reached Islamabad.

“Through extrajudicial killings, an example of lawlessness is being set. The series of extrajudicial killings may one day reach political workers,” he warned.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: PM Shehbaz forms body to review proposed LPG policy reforms
description: Policy seeks to shift LPG imports and pricing from Ogra to SOEs, which will adopt import-parity rates based on Saudi Aramco prices and actual import costs.
author: Khaleeq Kiani
article_text:
• Policy seeks to shift LPG imports and price-setting from Ogra to SOEs• State-owned enterprises to introduce import-parity pricing based on Saudi Aramco rates and actual import costs

ISLAMABAD: Amid soaring prices following supply disruptions, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has constituted an eight-member ministerial committee to review a set of policy changes proposed by the Petroleum Division for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

The proposed reforms envisage allowing state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to enter the LPG import business and take over price-setting from the regulator, with prices subsequently passed on to the private sector.

The committee was constituted after LPG stakeholders, including marketing companies and dealers, protested against the finalisation of the new LPG policy without consulting them. The policy was earlier scheduled to come into force within a week.

Stakeholders said SOEs had limited LPG import experience and warned that the proposed levy on locally produced LPG would push prices higher, calling for a greater private-sector role.

LPG prices in the market range between Rs6,000 and Rs7,200 per 11.57kg cylinder, according to reported market rates, compared with the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority’s (Ogra) notified price of Rs3,296, as operations at the Iran border came to a halt earlier this month and imports through sea routes declined.

The committee, headed by the petroleum minister, will include the ministers for economic affairs and information, the PM’s adviser on interprovincial coordination, special assistant on energy, petroleum secretary, DG liquefied gases and head of the Government Relations Unit (GRU).

The committee has one month to review the proposed LPG reforms, cylinder standards and local LPG model, and submit a comprehensive report to the prime minister.

A cabinet summary, seen by Dawn, proposes retaining monthly LPG pricing but removing Ogra’s role, with SOEs, including PSO, Sui companies, PARCO and Pakistan LNG, leading the shift to import-parity pricing.

Under the proposal, SOEs would import LPG in bulk and set monthly prices based on Saudi Aramco’s FOB rates, plus actual premiums, freight, insurance, incidental expenses and import taxes incurred in the previous month. “Given the urgency and need for greater participation by larger market players, it is being proposed that financial offers by the bidders would not be published on the PPRA website (exemption), in line with general market practice,” the summary stated.

It also proposed that Ogra immediately stop issuing price notifications for locally produced and imported LPG.

The summary proposed keeping the monthly producer price linked to Saudi Aramco’s current-month contract price (CP) on an FOB basis, with adjustments according to the propane-butane ratio. Local producers would be entitled to receive only this producer price, while the difference between the Saudi CP-linked producer price and PSO’s base price would be deposited into a dedicated fund to subsidise poor consumers through the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP).

The private sector wants to end Saudi CP-linked pricing, arguing that most LPG imports come from countries such as Iran and Oman.

When SOEs do not import LPG, the previous month’s premiums, incidental costs and taxes would apply alongside the current month’s CP, as in the pricing mechanism for petrol and diesel.

The summary also proposed increasing the margins of LPG marketing and importing companies to a minimum of Rs50,000 per tonne from the existing Rs35,000 per tonne. The increase has been proposed as an inflation adjustment to margins that have remained unchanged since the 2016 LPG policy. However, the revised margins would remain subject to competition.

The Competition Commission of Pakistan and Ogra would be responsible for preventing collusion among industry players.

The proposal also calls for a Producer-Price Differential Fund, with refineries and other producers depositing the difference between local and imported LPG prices into a dedicated Public Account.

The fund would be audited by the Auditor General of Pakistan and used by the federal government to provide targeted subsidies to vulnerable LPG consumers through the BISP scorecard.

The proposal allocates 10pc of locally produced LPG to state-owned marketers at producer prices to supply Gilgit-Baltistan, Northern Areas and other remote regions through cylinders and existing air-mix plants.

The remaining 90pc would be allocated to prequalified bottlers through transparent monthly auctions, with a floor price set at five per cent of PSO’s import-parity price.

article_html:
• Policy seeks to shift LPG imports and price-setting from Ogra to SOEs
• State-owned enterprises to introduce import-parity pricing based on Saudi Aramco rates and actual import costs

ISLAMABAD: Amid soaring prices following supply disruptions, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has constituted an eight-member ministerial committee to review a set of policy changes proposed by the Petroleum Division for liquefied petroleum gas (LPG).

The proposed reforms envisage allowing state-owned enterprises (SOEs) to enter the LPG import business and take over price-setting from the regulator, with prices subsequently passed on to the private sector.

The committee was constituted after LPG stakeholders, including marketing companies and dealers, protested against the finalisation of the new LPG policy without consulting them. The policy was earlier scheduled to come into force within a week.

Stakeholders said SOEs had limited LPG import experience and warned that the proposed levy on locally produced LPG would push prices higher, calling for a greater private-sector role.

LPG prices in the market range between Rs6,000 and Rs7,200 per 11.57kg cylinder, according to reported market rates, compared with the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority’s (Ogra) notified price of Rs3,296, as operations at the Iran border came to a halt earlier this month and imports through sea routes declined.

The committee, headed by the petroleum minister, will include the ministers for economic affairs and information, the PM’s adviser on interprovincial coordination, special assistant on energy, petroleum secretary, DG liquefied gases and head of the Government Relations Unit (GRU).

The committee has one month to review the proposed LPG reforms, cylinder standards and local LPG model, and submit a comprehensive report to the prime minister.

A cabinet summary, seen by Dawn, proposes retaining monthly LPG pricing but removing Ogra’s role, with SOEs, including PSO, Sui companies, PARCO and Pakistan LNG, leading the shift to import-parity pricing.

Under the proposal, SOEs would import LPG in bulk and set monthly prices based on Saudi Aramco’s FOB rates, plus actual premiums, freight, insurance, incidental expenses and import taxes incurred in the previous month. “Given the urgency and need for greater participation by larger market players, it is being proposed that financial offers by the bidders would not be published on the PPRA website (exemption), in line with general market practice,” the summary stated.

It also proposed that Ogra immediately stop issuing price notifications for locally produced and imported LPG.

The summary proposed keeping the monthly producer price linked to Saudi Aramco’s current-month contract price (CP) on an FOB basis, with adjustments according to the propane-butane ratio. Local producers would be entitled to receive only this producer price, while the difference between the Saudi CP-linked producer price and PSO’s base price would be deposited into a dedicated fund to subsidise poor consumers through the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP).

The private sector wants to end Saudi CP-linked pricing, arguing that most LPG imports come from countries such as Iran and Oman.

When SOEs do not import LPG, the previous month’s premiums, incidental costs and taxes would apply alongside the current month’s CP, as in the pricing mechanism for petrol and diesel.

The summary also proposed increasing the margins of LPG marketing and importing companies to a minimum of Rs50,000 per tonne from the existing Rs35,000 per tonne. The increase has been proposed as an inflation adjustment to margins that have remained unchanged since the 2016 LPG policy. However, the revised margins would remain subject to competition.

The Competition Commission of Pakistan and Ogra would be responsible for preventing collusion among industry players.

The proposal also calls for a Producer-Price Differential Fund, with refineries and other producers depositing the difference between local and imported LPG prices into a dedicated Public Account.

The fund would be audited by the Auditor General of Pakistan and used by the federal government to provide targeted subsidies to vulnerable LPG consumers through the BISP scorecard.

The proposal allocates 10pc of locally produced LPG to state-owned marketers at producer prices to supply Gilgit-Baltistan, Northern Areas and other remote regions through cylinders and existing air-mix plants.

The remaining 90pc would be allocated to prequalified bottlers through transparent monthly auctions, with a floor price set at five per cent of PSO’s import-parity price.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: Oil and Gas Development Company Ltd profit surges to Rs58.5bn
description: ISLAMABAD: Oil and Gas Development Company Ltd (OGDCL) on Friday announced that its profit after tax surged 52.7 per...
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
ISLAMABAD: Oil and Gas Development Company Ltd (OGDCL) on Friday announced that its profit after tax surged 52.7 per cent to Rs58.5 billion in the first quarter of 2026-27, supported by elevated international prices and higher oil and gas output.

As a consequence, the board of directors of the country’s largest exploration and production company announced an interim cash dividend of Rs5 per share, its highest-ever first-quarter payout to shareholders, up from Rs3.50 per share a year earlier.

The company’s net sales revenue rose 38pc to Rs132.4 billion from Rs96.2bn in the corresponding quarter, and PAT to Rs58.5bn from Rs38.3bn, lifting earnings per share to Rs13.60 from Rs8.91.

The improvement was driven by higher production volumes and stronger realised prices, which was partly offset by continued forced production curtailments and the appreciation of the rupee against the US dollar.

Collections against billings stood at 100pc for the quarter. OGDCL contributed Rs82bn to the national exchequer thro­ugh taxes, dividends, royalties and levies, and its indigenous oil and gas production saved the country an estimated $1.32­bn in foreign exchange through import substitution.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: ANP announces MPC over Asghar Achakzai’s arrest
description: ANP president says all political parties, members of the legal fraternity and traders’ associations would be formally invited to attend the conference.
author: Muhammad Akbar Notezai
article_text:
QUETTA: Acting president of the Awami National Party (ANP), Balochistan, Jamaluddin Rishtya, strongly condemned the arrest of the party’s provincial president, Asghar Khan Achakzai, describing the charges against him as fake, baseless and fabricated.

Addressing a press conference at the Quetta Press Club on Friday, Mr Rishtya announced that a multi-party conference (MPC) would be convened in Quetta on

Nov 6 to decide the party’s future course of action. He said all political parties, members of the legal fraternity and traders’ associations would be formally invited to attend the conference.

Mr Rishtya reiterated that the party would not abandon the non-violent philosophy of Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (Bacha Khan) or its struggle for the rights of oppressed nations in response to such “cheap tactics”.

“The Awami National Party believes in the respect, freedom and autonomy of the judiciary and the rule of law, and our leaders have sacrificed their lives for these principles,” Mr Rishtya said.

Smoke-emitting vehicles fined in Lahore
description: Authorities inspect 2,018 industrial units across Lahore division, seal 41 units and 146 restaurants for causing pollution.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
LAHORE: During the current month in Lahore, as many as 1,763 smoke-emitting vehicles were fined, while a total penalty of Rs5.5 million was imposed.

During the same period, 739 vehicles were impounded and overloaded vehicles were offloaded in Lahore.

Furthermore, 2,018 industrial units were inspected across the Lahore division, resulting in 41 units and 146 restaurants being sealed for causing pollution.

Action was also taken at 49 locations in the division against burning crop residues. Consequently, eight FIRs were registered and a fine of Rs240,000 was imposed for burning crop remains. These details were shared during a meeting presided over by Lahore Commissioner Nauman Yousuf.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: Canada, EU launch new alliance with deals on Ukraine, minerals, AI
description: MONTREAL: The EU and Canada announced an alliance on Friday aimed at cementing their own relations in the face of...
author: AFP
article_text:
MONTREAL: The EU and Canada announced an alliance on Friday aimed at cementing their own relations in the face of President Donald Trump’s moves to tear up US ties with its old partners.

After a two-day summit in Montreal, the EU said Canada will join a 90 billion euro ($103bn) support loan for Ukraine and work closely with Brussels on anything from critical minerals to artificial intelligence.

“The world’s becoming more dangerous and divided. Our societies are being shaken by new storms,” Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney told a press conference, mentioning eroding democratic norms and “the weaponisation of trade”.

“Together, Canada and the European Union are anchoring the ground. Anchoring our ground to uphold our values while forming a protective canopy under which our citizens can all thrive,” he said after talks with EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

Already sharing a free trade agreement, Canada and the EU have sought to move closer together since Trump’s shock return to power.

Both Canada and the EU have been hit with US tariffs and territorial threats. Ahead of the talks on Friday, Von der Leyen, the European Commission’s president, said Canada could not become a “full-fledged” EU member due to its geographical location, but the bloc wanted to bring it “as close as possible”.

Carney said Canada will join the EU’s 90bn euro support loan for Ukraine with an initial participation of 500 million euros.

The announcement comes at a time when Brussels is looking for help to plug gaps in Kyiv’s finances.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: Excessive punishment
description: It is unfortunate to see her and her husband punished so harshly for acts that seem downright frivolous compared to the violence actual terrorists routinely perpetrate.
author: Editorial
article_text:
THE supposed ‘crime’ did not justify a trial under terrorism laws, and certainly not the punishment. On Thursday, human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari-Hazir and her husband and fellow lawyer, Hadi Ali Chattha, were sentenced to 10 years each for moving a security barrier reportedly placed to protect a touring cricket team, as well as for “incitement to public unrest” during a face-off with police.

The trial, held in jail, drew persistent criticism over an alleged lack of due process. The judge held that Ms Mazari-Hazir and Mr Chattha had attempted to “compromise the security arrangements [made for the team] through pressuring security officials”.

The judgement cited the 2009 attack on the Sri Lankan cricket team in Lahore — an assault that had been perpetrated by more than a dozen terrorists armed with heavy weapons — to reason that the lawyers’ act of removing the barrier and ‘assaulting’ police personnel “put the security of an international team visiting Pakistan at risk [and] clearly shows the intentions and objective of the accused to create sense of terror [sic]”.

Just last month, after a lengthy appeals process, the Supreme Court ordered the suspension of the sentence handed to the two lawyers in the so-called social media posts case and ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s decision on their appeal against the trial court’s verdict.

However, they were promptly rearrested in connection with this case, and have now been handed a lengthy sentence that will keep them behind bars while they appeal. Ms Mazari-Hazir is one of the most prominent champions of civil and human rights from the legal community, and has often taken cases involving some of Pakistan’s most vulnerable citizens pro bono.

She is also an outspoken critic of government and state excesses. It is unfortunate to see her and her husband punished so harshly for acts that seem downright frivolous compared to the violence actual terrorists routinely perpetrate.

The higher courts must hear their appeal swiftly, and the state must stop stretching antiterrorism laws to cover acts that bear no resemblance to terrorism. Such verdicts send a chilling message to every lawyer willing to defend the vulnerable. The law need only appear to serve narrow interests, rather than justice, for public faith in it to be shaken.

THE supposed ‘crime’ did not justify a trial under terrorism laws, and certainly not the punishment. On Thursday, human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari-Hazir and her husband and fellow lawyer, Hadi Ali Chattha, were sentenced to 10 years each for moving a security barrier reportedly placed to protect a touring cricket team, as well as for “incitement to public unrest” during a face-off with police.

The trial, held in jail, drew persistent criticism over an alleged lack of due process. The judge held that Ms Mazari-Hazir and Mr Chattha had attempted to “compromise the security arrangements [made for the team] through pressuring security officials”.

The judgement cited the 2009 attack on the Sri Lankan cricket team in Lahore — an assault that had been perpetrated by more than a dozen terrorists armed with heavy weapons — to reason that the lawyers’ act of removing the barrier and ‘assaulting’ police personnel “put the security of an international team visiting Pakistan at risk [and] clearly shows the intentions and objective of the accused to create sense of terror [sic]”.

Just last month, after a lengthy appeals process, the Supreme Court ordered the suspension of the sentence handed to the two lawyers in the so-called social media posts case and ordered their release pending the Islamabad High Court’s decision on their appeal against the trial court’s verdict.

However, they were promptly rearrested in connection with this case, and have now been handed a lengthy sentence that will keep them behind bars while they appeal. Ms Mazari-Hazir is one of the most prominent champions of civil and human rights from the legal community, and has often taken cases involving some of Pakistan’s most vulnerable citizens pro bono.

She is also an outspoken critic of government and state excesses. It is unfortunate to see her and her husband punished so harshly for acts that seem downright frivolous compared to the violence actual terrorists routinely perpetrate.

The higher courts must hear their appeal swiftly, and the state must stop stretching antiterrorism laws to cover acts that bear no resemblance to terrorism. Such verdicts send a chilling message to every lawyer willing to defend the vulnerable. The law need only appear to serve narrow interests, rather than justice, for public faith in it to be shaken.

On Thursday, human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari-Hazir and her husband and fellow lawyer, Hadi Ali Chattha, were sentenced to 10 years each for moving a security barrier reportedly placed to protect a touring cricket team, as well as for “incitement to public unrest” during a face-off with police.

headline: Pakistan’s reforms deficit
description: Reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.
author: Tahsin Shah
article_text:
PAKISTAN has never suffered from a shortage of civil service reform proposals. It has suffered from a shortage of reforms that survive implementation.

Since independence, successive governments, commissions and committees have attempted to restructure the administrative machinery inherited from the colonial state. Yet familiar complaints persist: excessive generalism, weak accountability, politicisation, distorted incentives, slow decision-making and a bureaucracy often better equipped to process files than solve complex problems.

The latest reform package is significant not because Pakistan has rediscovered civil service reform, but because it attempts to address several structural weaknesses simultaneously.

It proposes 11 specialised professional cadres, competency-based recruitment, performance-linked remuneration, restructuring of training and human-resource management, and a National Executive Service (NES) under which BS-20 and above positions could be opened to serving officials, academics and private-sector professionals.

Pakistan inherited the powerful, generalist Civil Service of Pakistan from the colonial administrative tradition. The most dramatic restructuring came under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1973, when the CSP structure was abolished and occupational groups reorganised. But restructuring did not democratise opportunity within government.

The devolution reforms introduced under Gen Pervez Musharraf in 2001 represented another major intervention, transferring substantial authority towards elected local governments and altering traditional district administration. But institutional discontinuity and subsequent political changes prevented the system from developing into a durable architecture of local governance.

Reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.

This history reveals Pakistan’s recurring problem: reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.

The strongest feature of the present package is its recognition that a modern state cannot be managed through transferable generalists. Professional cadres in fields including IT and telecom, energy, climate, engineering, health, education, law, agriculture and science address a genuine administrative weakness.

Opening senior positions to competition could be still more consequential. It could bring specialists into government who would otherwise never enter conventional public service and allow capable career officers to compete beyond rigid cadre boundaries. But lateral entry carries an equally obvious risk: without credible safeguards, it can become lateral patronage.

International experience offers principles rather than readymade templates. Pakistan should borrow principles, not blindly transplant institutions.

Performance-linked remuneration illustrates the challenge. Annual performance agreements for ministries, flowing down to individual officers, could improve accountability. But who determines whether a secretary has performed well? If targets are vague or assessments depend excessively upon political superiors, financial incentives could rew­ard proximity to power rather than performance.

The ultimate measurement must therefore be governance. Does a business licence take days instead of months? Are teachers and doctors present? Are development projects completed on time? Can citizens obtain public services without intermediaries? Can civil servants make lawful professional decisions without seeking political protection?

Significantly, the Police Service and Foreign Service would remain outside the proposed NES. There are sound reasons for treating them as specialised career services requiring institutional continuity, accumulated professional experience and service-specific training. Their exclusion from the NES, however, need not mean exclusion from reform.

For the police, Pakistan does not need to start from scratch. In May 2018, then chief justice Mian Saqib Nisar initiated a Police Reforms Committee bringing together nine retired and seven serving Inspectors General of Police. After extensive deliberations, it produced the two-volume Police Reforms: Way Forward, launched in Jan 2019.

Building upon the Police Order 2002 and subsequent experience, the exercise addressed some of the most persistent weaknesses of policing: accountability, quality and independence of investigation, complaint redressal, urban policing, alternative dispute resolution, counterterrorism and the legal framework governing the police. It proposed a model police law while recognising the constitutional and administrative realities of Pakistan’s federal system.

Yet the principal structural problems identified by the committee remain largely unresolved. Its convener, former IGP Afzal Ali Shigri, observed as recently as Feb 2026 that fragmented legal frameworks, weaknesses in investigation and uneven accountability mechanisms continue to impede reform.

The 2019 police reform report thus stands as a telling case study of Pakistan’s persistent gap between designing reform and implementing it.

The exclusion of the Police Service from the NES presents an opportunity rather than necessarily a deficiency. Instead of forcing policing into an administrative model designed for civilian mi­­nistries, the government can revive Police Reforms: Way Forward, update it and implement its still-relevant recommendations. The Foreign Service can similarly retain its distinctive professional structure while pursuing the broader reform principles of merit, specialisation, transparent advancement and measurable performance.

The government proposes an ambitious implementation timetable for the new civil-service package. Speed can create momentum, but changing regulations is easier than changing administrative culture.

No examination reform can compensate for arbitrary postings. No specialised cadre can flourish if expertise is subordinated to connections. No performance contract creates accountability if influence protects poor performance. And no reform report, however professionally drafted, improves governance while it remains on a shelf.

Pakistan has spent decades reforming bureaucracy on paper. The real reform is to build institutions where competence matters more than cadre, performance more than seniority, expertise more than connections and public service more than institutional privilege.

The writer is a former Inspector General of Police and DG FIA.

article_html:
PAKISTAN has never suffered from a shortage of civil service reform proposals. It has suffered from a shortage of reforms that survive implementation.

Since independence, successive governments, commissions and committees have attempted to restructure the administrative machinery inherited from the colonial state. Yet familiar complaints persist: excessive generalism, weak accountability, politicisation, distorted incentives, slow decision-making and a bureaucracy often better equipped to process files than solve complex problems.

The latest reform package is significant not because Pakistan has rediscovered civil service reform, but because it attempts to address several structural weaknesses simultaneously.

It proposes 11 specialised professional cadres, competency-based recruitment, performance-linked remuneration, restructuring of training and human-resource management, and a National Executive Service (NES) under which BS-20 and above positions could be opened to serving officials, academics and private-sector professionals.

Pakistan inherited the powerful, generalist Civil Service of Pakistan from the colonial administrative tradition. The most dramatic restructuring came under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1973, when the CSP structure was abolished and occupational groups reorganised. But restructuring did not democratise opportunity within government.

The devolution reforms introduced under Gen Pervez Musharraf in 2001 represented another major intervention, transferring substantial authority towards elected local governments and altering traditional district administration. But institutional discontinuity and subsequent political changes prevented the system from developing into a durable architecture of local governance.

Reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.

This history reveals Pakistan’s recurring problem: reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.

The strongest feature of the present package is its recognition that a modern state cannot be managed through transferable generalists. Professional cadres in fields including IT and telecom, energy, climate, engineering, health, education, law, agriculture and science address a genuine administrative weakness.

Opening senior positions to competition could be still more consequential. It could bring specialists into government who would otherwise never enter conventional public service and allow capable career officers to compete beyond rigid cadre boundaries. But lateral entry carries an equally obvious risk: without credible safeguards, it can become lateral patronage.

International experience offers principles rather than readymade templates. Pakistan should borrow principles, not blindly transplant institutions.

Performance-linked remuneration illustrates the challenge. Annual performance agreements for ministries, flowing down to individual officers, could improve accountability. But who determines whether a secretary has performed well? If targets are vague or assessments depend excessively upon political superiors, financial incentives could rew­ard proximity to power rather than performance.

The ultimate measurement must therefore be governance. Does a business licence take days instead of months? Are teachers and doctors present? Are development projects completed on time? Can citizens obtain public services without intermediaries? Can civil servants make lawful professional decisions without seeking political protection?

Significantly, the Police Service and Foreign Service would remain outside the proposed NES. There are sound reasons for treating them as specialised career services requiring institutional continuity, accumulated professional experience and service-specific training. Their exclusion from the NES, however, need not mean exclusion from reform.

For the police, Pakistan does not need to start from scratch. In May 2018, then chief justice Mian Saqib Nisar initiated a Police Reforms Committee bringing together nine retired and seven serving Inspectors General of Police. After extensive deliberations, it produced the two-volume Police Reforms: Way Forward, launched in Jan 2019.

Building upon the Police Order 2002 and subsequent experience, the exercise addressed some of the most persistent weaknesses of policing: accountability, quality and independence of investigation, complaint redressal, urban policing, alternative dispute resolution, counterterrorism and the legal framework governing the police. It proposed a model police law while recognising the constitutional and administrative realities of Pakistan’s federal system.

Yet the principal structural problems identified by the committee remain largely unresolved. Its convener, former IGP Afzal Ali Shigri, observed as recently as Feb 2026 that fragmented legal frameworks, weaknesses in investigation and uneven accountability mechanisms continue to impede reform.

The 2019 police reform report thus stands as a telling case study of Pakistan’s persistent gap between designing reform and implementing it.

The exclusion of the Police Service from the NES presents an opportunity rather than necessarily a deficiency. Instead of forcing policing into an administrative model designed for civilian mi­­nistries, the government can revive Police Reforms: Way Forward, update it and implement its still-relevant recommendations. The Foreign Service can similarly retain its distinctive professional structure while pursuing the broader reform principles of merit, specialisation, transparent advancement and measurable performance.

The government proposes an ambitious implementation timetable for the new civil-service package. Speed can create momentum, but changing regulations is easier than changing administrative culture.

No examination reform can compensate for arbitrary postings. No specialised cadre can flourish if expertise is subordinated to connections. No performance contract creates accountability if influence protects poor performance. And no reform report, however professionally drafted, improves governance while it remains on a shelf.

Pakistan has spent decades reforming bureaucracy on paper. The real reform is to build institutions where competence matters more than cadre, performance more than seniority, expertise more than connections and public service more than institutional privilege.

The writer is a former Inspector General of Police and DG FIA.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

article_html:
PAKISTAN has never suffered from a shortage of civil service reform proposals. It has suffered from a shortage of reforms that survive implementation.

Since independence, successive governments, commissions and committees have attempted to restructure the administrative machinery inherited from the colonial state. Yet familiar complaints persist: excessive generalism, weak accountability, politicisation, distorted incentives, slow decision-making and a bureaucracy often better equipped to process files than solve complex problems.

The latest reform package is significant not because Pakistan has rediscovered civil service reform, but because it attempts to address several structural weaknesses simultaneously.

It proposes 11 specialised professional cadres, competency-based recruitment, performance-linked remuneration, restructuring of training and human-resource management, and a National Executive Service (NES) under which BS-20 and above positions could be opened to serving officials, academics and private-sector professionals.

Pakistan inherited the powerful, generalist Civil Service of Pakistan from the colonial administrative tradition. The most dramatic restructuring came under Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1973, when the CSP structure was abolished and occupational groups reorganised. But restructuring did not democratise opportunity within government.

The devolution reforms introduced under Gen Pervez Musharraf in 2001 represented another major intervention, transferring substantial authority towards elected local governments and altering traditional district administration. But institutional discontinuity and subsequent political changes prevented the system from developing into a durable architecture of local governance.

Reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.

This history reveals Pakistan’s recurring problem: reform is often treated as an event rather than a sustained process.

The strongest feature of the present package is its recognition that a modern state cannot be managed through transferable generalists. Professional cadres in fields including IT and telecom, energy, climate, engineering, health, education, law, agriculture and science address a genuine administrative weakness.

Opening senior positions to competition could be still more consequential. It could bring specialists into government who would otherwise never enter conventional public service and allow capable career officers to compete beyond rigid cadre boundaries. But lateral entry carries an equally obvious risk: without credible safeguards, it can become lateral patronage.

International experience offers principles rather than readymade templates. Pakistan should borrow principles, not blindly transplant institutions.

Performance-linked remuneration illustrates the challenge. Annual performance agreements for ministries, flowing down to individual officers, could improve accountability. But who determines whether a secretary has performed well? If targets are vague or assessments depend excessively upon political superiors, financial incentives could rew­ard proximity to power rather than performance.

The ultimate measurement must therefore be governance. Does a business licence take days instead of months? Are teachers and doctors present? Are development projects completed on time? Can citizens obtain public services without intermediaries? Can civil servants make lawful professional decisions without seeking political protection?

Significantly, the Police Service and Foreign Service would remain outside the proposed NES. There are sound reasons for treating them as specialised career services requiring institutional continuity, accumulated professional experience and service-specific training. Their exclusion from the NES, however, need not mean exclusion from reform.

For the police, Pakistan does not need to start from scratch. In May 2018, then chief justice Mian Saqib Nisar initiated a Police Reforms Committee bringing together nine retired and seven serving Inspectors General of Police. After extensive deliberations, it produced the two-volume Police Reforms: Way Forward, launched in Jan 2019.

Building upon the Police Order 2002 and subsequent experience, the exercise addressed some of the most persistent weaknesses of policing: accountability, quality and independence of investigation, complaint redressal, urban policing, alternative dispute resolution, counterterrorism and the legal framework governing the police. It proposed a model police law while recognising the constitutional and administrative realities of Pakistan’s federal system.

Yet the principal structural problems identified by the committee remain largely unresolved. Its convener, former IGP Afzal Ali Shigri, observed as recently as Feb 2026 that fragmented legal frameworks, weaknesses in investigation and uneven accountability mechanisms continue to impede reform.

The 2019 police reform report thus stands as a telling case study of Pakistan’s persistent gap between designing reform and implementing it.

The exclusion of the Police Service from the NES presents an opportunity rather than necessarily a deficiency. Instead of forcing policing into an administrative model designed for civilian mi­­nistries, the government can revive Police Reforms: Way Forward, update it and implement its still-relevant recommendations. The Foreign Service can similarly retain its distinctive professional structure while pursuing the broader reform principles of merit, specialisation, transparent advancement and measurable performance.

The government proposes an ambitious implementation timetable for the new civil-service package. Speed can create momentum, but changing regulations is easier than changing administrative culture.

No examination reform can compensate for arbitrary postings. No specialised cadre can flourish if expertise is subordinated to connections. No performance contract creates accountability if influence protects poor performance. And no reform report, however professionally drafted, improves governance while it remains on a shelf.

Pakistan has spent decades reforming bureaucracy on paper. The real reform is to build institutions where competence matters more than cadre, performance more than seniority, expertise more than connections and public service more than institutional privilege.

The writer is a former Inspector General of Police and DG FIA.

headline: The cost of injustice
description: Diseased societies produce diseased people.
author: Rafia Zakaria
article_text:
TO live in Karachi, or really any city in the tumultuous world that is our reality, is an exercise in dodging misfortune. When one leaves the house, one braces for survival. Traffic has to be navigated, angry or errant drivers avoided, beggars ask for money and there is filth on the street. By the time one reaches the destination, one is in a state of high vigilance. Dangers and disruptions are everywhere.

This means that most in the city live in a constant state of hypervigilance. Some would say that wealth can insulate a person from this avalanche of potential misfortune. There is material evidence of this: the wealthy have drivers who take them places, their cars and homes are cool with air conditioning and electricity outages are eliminated with generators.

They see the best doctors and eat the best food. If you belong to this class, the injustice that you see everywhere in a megacity is made distant. The maimed beggar, the dog being beaten, the woman wrapped in black trying to navigate a street full of men are things that exist in some different world.

The car window, the tall gate, the armed guard — these, it is assumed, make the cruelties of the context irrelevant. If they are considered, it is only in a calculation that assures you that your good fortune is deserved and those suffering must have earned it through some arithmetic of divine distribution.

The truth is that life in an unjust society exacts a cost. It does not matter how well you may take care of yourself; context matters. In her extraordinary book Weathering: The Extraordinary Stress of Ordinary Life in an Unjust Society, Dr Arline Geronimus has shown that the constant physical toll of coping with injustice can have deep physical and mental consequences. Naturally, the most disadvantaged suffer the worst consequences, but the effects of living amid inequality accrue on everyone in a society.

Diseased societies produce diseased people.

One category of disadvantaged people in Pakistani society is women. In a world in which patriarchy reigns, women are always playing defence. Marriage is a minefield where, if the demands of a husband or in laws are not met, every day can become a living hell.

A long list of dead women that I regularly write about in this column is evidence of this. If a woman is unable to bear a child for instance, she may either face divorce or her husband taking a second wife. If children do come, they can increase a woman’s dependence on her husband, making it harder to resist whatever strictures are imposed upon her.

The cost of all this is a constant state of vigilance, and Geronimus showed just how it can physically wear one down. Repeated activation of the stress response can disrupt hormonal regulation, raise blood pressure and contribute to inflammation. In the long term, this increases vulnerability to chronic disease and early death. Diseased societies produce diseased people.

A 2021 systematic study and meta-analysis found that 37 per cent of pregnant women experienced antenatal depression, while 30pc experienced postnatal depression. Intimate partner violence and poor relationships with spouses were among the reported risk factors. These figures can be attributed to the fact that women do not feel confident about their own or their children’s futures because they live in a society where injustice is common.

The most interesting thing about research on men and women in unjust societies is that men suffer too. Research examining sexism in US states has linked patriarchal contexts to poorer health outcomes in both men and women.

People believe that individual actions, status or material wealth can allow them to ev­­ade the conditions they see others endure. All this suggests that individual choices and we­­alth are not the biggest determinants of health in a society. Instead, it is the availability of collective justice and respect for life that affect health outcomes. This should give all Pakistanis pause. The poor are treated horribly, and we see terrible crimes committed against the weak every day. Women are regularly treated like chattel, children are routinely abused and caste and wealth determine the course of one’s life.

The worst curse is that we have learned to rationalise all of this, to absorb it as the way things are, the way things have been and the way things will always be. But being inured to injustice and quietly accepting of it is making us sick. Our tolerance of it creeps into our cells and our bones.

It is time we understood that there is no individual cure for these conditions and what ails us is a collective issue — deeper and more entrenched than improving our diets, quitting smoking or hitting the gym. Our habit of seeing so many wrongs and ignoring them is quite literally what is killing us.

The writer is an attorney teaching constitutional law and political philosophy.

In her extraordinary book Weathering: The Extraordinary Stress of Ordinary Life in an Unjust Society, Dr Arline Geronimus has shown that the constant physical toll of coping with injustice can have deep physical and mental consequences. Naturally, the most disadvantaged suffer the worst consequences, but the effects of living amid inequality accrue on everyone in a society.

A 2021 systematic study and meta-analysis found that 37 per cent of pregnant women experienced antenatal depression, while 30pc experienced postnatal depression. Intimate partner violence and poor relationships with spouses were among the reported risk factors. These figures can be attributed to the fact that women do not feel confident about their own or their children’s futures because they live in a society where injustice is common.

The most interesting thing about research on men and women in unjust societies is that men suffer too. Research examining sexism in US states has linked patriarchal contexts to poorer health outcomes in both men and women.

People believe that individual actions, status or material wealth can allow them to ev­­ade the conditions they see others endure. All this suggests that individual choices and we­­alth are not the biggest determinants of health in a society. Instead, it is the availability of collective justice and respect for life that affect health outcomes. This should give all Pakistanis pause. The poor are treated horribly, and we see terrible crimes committed against the weak every day. Women are regularly treated like chattel, children are routinely abused and caste and wealth determine the course of one’s life.

The worst curse is that we have learned to rationalise all of this, to absorb it as the way things are, the way things have been and the way things will always be. But being inured to injustice and quietly accepting of it is making us sick. Our tolerance of it creeps into our cells and our bones.

It is time we understood that there is no individual cure for these conditions and what ails us is a collective issue — deeper and more entrenched than improving our diets, quitting smoking or hitting the gym. Our habit of seeing so many wrongs and ignoring them is quite literally what is killing us.

headline: SHC moved against construction on Karachi's Nehr-i-Khayyam
description: Jamaat-i-Islami and three other petitioners seek an immediate halt to construction and the restoration of Nehr-i-Khayyam as a stormwater drain.
author: Ishaq Tanoli
article_text:
KARACHI: The Jamaat-i-Islami, along with some Clifton residents, moved the Sindh High Court against the provincial government for carrying out construction and development activities on Nehr-i-Khayyam.

Leader of the Opposition in the City Council Advocate Saifuddin and three others filed a petition, citing the chief secretary, local government secretary, Karachi Metropolitan Corporation, Karachi Development Authority, Karachi Water & Sewage Corporation, Sindh Environmental Protection Agency and Boat Basin SHO as respondents.

They submitted in the petition that they were aggrieved by the ongoing construction and development activities being carried out in and around Nehr-i-Khayyam in Clifton including adjacent amenity plots, which has raised serious concerns about preservation of the natural waterway, potential adverse impact upon city’s rainwater drainage system and the possible commercial utilisation of land of such waterway.

They also contended that the construction, alteration and development were being carried out rapidly on the subject waterway and the mega project was being proceeded without a proper technical and environmental assessment, which may adversely affect the flow of rainwater, particularly during the monsoon season, thereby endangering public safety and the civic interests of residents of Karachi.

They further stated that the respondents could not lawfully disregard the approved planning framework or permit development inconsistent with the designated purpose of the watercourse and its associated public infrastructure.

Referring to previous judgements of the Supreme Court and the SHC, the petitioners maintained that the judiciary had stopped the construction in the vicinity of Nehr-i-Khayyam on a number of occasions, but after reported suspension of construction for a brief period, such activities had time and again been resumed.

The petitioners maintained that if these construction activities were allowed to continue without lawful authority, adequate technical assessment and compliance with the applicable environmental safeguards, the same would threaten the effective functioning of an essential storm-water drainage facility and expose the residents to risks of flooding and environmental degradation.

They asked the SHC to declare as illegal the alleged conversion, alteration or utilisation of the storm-water drain into a recreational park or commercial venture or any other inconsistent purpose without lawful authority and compliance with the applicable laws.

They urged the court to preserve Nehr-i-Khayyam for its lawful purpose and primary function as a storm-water drainage channel.

They also sought directives to immediately halt all ongoing construction and development activities and remove all structures, encroachments, unauthorised constructions, reclaimed portions and other works already erected or undertaken within the lawful boundaries of Nehr-i-Khayyam.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026

headline: Commuters risk life and limb as poles not removed from middle of road in Hyderabad
description: CM Murad says carriageway carpeted and opened to force Hesco into relocating transmission lines.
author: Mohammad Hussain Khan
article_text:
HYDERABAD: Carpeting of a new road and opening it for traffic, despite many electricity poles still standing in the middle of the dual carriageway, has triggered a heated debate on social media as travelers risk life and limb.

Responding to the criticism from people, the Sindh government defended its decision to complete and open the road — connecting Alamdar Chowk with the old National Highway near Qasim Chowk — saying that the Hyderabad Electric Supply Company (Hesco) had been showing lethargy in fulfilling its responsibility of relocating the poles after which such a decision was taken.

The poles carry high-tension lines emanating from near the 132-kV grid station of Qasimabad that feeds a considerably large part of Hyderabad city.

Social media users had uploaded videos of the road dotted with the poles a couple of days back with crispy comments.

CM says carriageway carpeted and opened to force Hesco into relocating transmission lines

The poles existed in their place when the road was being given the first layer of carpeting. Since the two ends of the road were not blocked with barriers, vehicles started plying along it supposing that there was no risk in using it. However, the poles posed a great risk to commuters’ life. Motorists and bike-riders have to drive in a zig-zag manner to avoid hitting the poles.

On Friday, the criticism forced Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah to publicly explain that it was Hesco’s responsibility to relocate the poles. The power utility was provided funds for the work, but it did not carry out the work, he said while speaking at the inaugural ceremony of the World Culture Festival in Karachi.

The chief minister said there was a major issue of land availability for the construction of the road. The chief secretary, he said, contacted the military estate authorities and got the land use permission.

He explained that as a matter of strategy, the government constructed the road first and restored the traffic so that pressure would come upon Hesco. He pointed out: “As soon as the road was constructed, public pressure increased and Hesco was forced to remove the poles”.

The road is a 1.6km-long dual carriageway which is part of three road projects involving a cost of Rs1.06 billion. It is entirely new for the people of Hyderabad and connects the city’s bypass from the Qasim Chowk road.

Until now used to be known as Ghora Ground, the artery has been converted to an asphalt road, the landscape otherwise being an abandoned waterlogged area used for electricity transmission to Deh Fouj Gah through the poles. The area is located within the administrative territory of the Cantonment Board Hyderabad and Military Estate Office (MEO).

Chief Secretary Sindh Asif Hyder Shah had obtained permission from the two offices to build this road in order to lessen the traffic pressure on Qasim Chowk and Wadhu Wah in Qasimabad. The work on the road project had begun in April this year.

Hyderabad mayor’s spokesman and district administration also had to respond to the criticism from people on social media. Sindh government’s spokesman Sadia Javed clarified the situation, but admitted that there was some sort of negligence seen on the part of the administration and that it should have put up barricades there with warning signs for commuters.

“When development schemes are executed, some issues do crop up,” she maintained.

According to Hesco spokesman Sadiq Kubar, Qasimabad grid station located near Alamdar Chowk feeds electricity to 27 feeders. Of them, 24 pass through this area which used to be an abandoned space until the road scheme was approved.

He said that out of the 27 feeders, 22 have been shifted to new poles and accordingly energised. The remaining five would also be energized, he added. Similarly, he explained, 100 high-transmission lines needed to be shifted and out of them, 50 were positioned in the area until this road project was conceived. He said that relocation of the poles involved a cost of Rs79m. He said that while these 50 poles stood removed from the road, as many others were located along the grid station.

Hyderabad Deputy Commissioner Zainul Abedin Memon, in his response to the issue on Thursday night, said that the road was not formally opened.

He claimed that barricades, cautionary signage and other deterrents were deployed by the executive agency concerned and the traffic police, “but commuters continue to breach them daily”.

He said proximity of Qasimabad grid station with the road necessitated relocation of electricity infrastructure, adding that until Wednesday (Oct 28), 97 poles had been shifted and the remaining ones would be relocated by Nov 10. He said only the ‘base binder course’ was laid; the final wearing (asphalt) course is yet to be laid. He said appropriate compaction is needed since it had previously been a waterlogged area. Thus, he added, ‘binder course’ is laid early.

article_html:
HYDERABAD: Carpeting of a new road and opening it for traffic, despite many electricity poles still standing in the middle of the dual carriageway, has triggered a heated debate on social media as travelers risk life and limb.

Responding to the criticism from people, the Sindh government defended its decision to complete and open the road — connecting Alamdar Chowk with the old National Highway near Qasim Chowk — saying that the Hyderabad Electric Supply Company (Hesco) had been showing lethargy in fulfilling its responsibility of relocating the poles after which such a decision was taken.

The poles carry high-tension lines emanating from near the 132-kV grid station of Qasimabad that feeds a considerably large part of Hyderabad city.

Social media users had uploaded videos of the road dotted with the poles a couple of days back with crispy comments.

CM says carriageway carpeted and opened to force Hesco into relocating transmission lines

The poles existed in their place when the road was being given the first layer of carpeting. Since the two ends of the road were not blocked with barriers, vehicles started plying along it supposing that there was no risk in using it. However, the poles posed a great risk to commuters’ life. Motorists and bike-riders have to drive in a zig-zag manner to avoid hitting the poles.

On Friday, the criticism forced Sindh Chief Minister Syed Murad Ali Shah to publicly explain that it was Hesco’s responsibility to relocate the poles. The power utility was provided funds for the work, but it did not carry out the work, he said while speaking at the inaugural ceremony of the World Culture Festival in Karachi.

The chief minister said there was a major issue of land availability for the construction of the road. The chief secretary, he said, contacted the military estate authorities and got the land use permission.

He explained that as a matter of strategy, the government constructed the road first and restored the traffic so that pressure would come upon Hesco. He pointed out: “As soon as the road was constructed, public pressure increased and Hesco was forced to remove the poles”.

The road is a 1.6km-long dual carriageway which is part of three road projects involving a cost of Rs1.06 billion. It is entirely new for the people of Hyderabad and connects the city’s bypass from the Qasim Chowk road.

Until now used to be known as Ghora Ground, the artery has been converted to an asphalt road, the landscape otherwise being an abandoned waterlogged area used for electricity transmission to Deh Fouj Gah through the poles. The area is located within the administrative territory of the Cantonment Board Hyderabad and Military Estate Office (MEO).

Chief Secretary Sindh Asif Hyder Shah had obtained permission from the two offices to build this road in order to lessen the traffic pressure on Qasim Chowk and Wadhu Wah in Qasimabad. The work on the road project had begun in April this year.

Hyderabad mayor’s spokesman and district administration also had to respond to the criticism from people on social media. Sindh government’s spokesman Sadia Javed clarified the situation, but admitted that there was some sort of negligence seen on the part of the administration and that it should have put up barricades there with warning signs for commuters.

“When development schemes are executed, some issues do crop up,” she maintained.

According to Hesco spokesman Sadiq Kubar, Qasimabad grid station located near Alamdar Chowk feeds electricity to 27 feeders. Of them, 24 pass through this area which used to be an abandoned space until the road scheme was approved.

He said that out of the 27 feeders, 22 have been shifted to new poles and accordingly energised. The remaining five would also be energized, he added. Similarly, he explained, 100 high-transmission lines needed to be shifted and out of them, 50 were positioned in the area until this road project was conceived. He said that relocation of the poles involved a cost of Rs79m. He said that while these 50 poles stood removed from the road, as many others were located along the grid station.

Hyderabad Deputy Commissioner Zainul Abedin Memon, in his response to the issue on Thursday night, said that the road was not formally opened.

He claimed that barricades, cautionary signage and other deterrents were deployed by the executive agency concerned and the traffic police, “but commuters continue to breach them daily”.

He said proximity of Qasimabad grid station with the road necessitated relocation of electricity infrastructure, adding that until Wednesday (Oct 28), 97 poles had been shifted and the remaining ones would be relocated by Nov 10. He said only the ‘base binder course’ was laid; the final wearing (asphalt) course is yet to be laid. He said appropriate compaction is needed since it had previously been a waterlogged area. Thus, he added, ‘binder course’ is laid early.

headline: Man held in Karachi for swindling, blackmailing woman via matrimonial app
description: The suspect allegedly obtained the money through online bank transfers and subsequently threatened the woman to circulate her doctored photographs on social media to extort further money.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
KARACHI: The National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) on Friday claimed to have arrested a man for allegedly depriving a woman of approximately Rs4.45 million by making empty promises of marriage on a matrimonial app.

According to the agency, the suspect, posing as “Hassam Uddin”, allegedly obtained the money through online bank transfers and subsequently threatened the woman to circulate her doctored photographs on social media to extort further money.

He was booked in a case under relevant sections of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, it added.

Initial investigations suggest that the suspect may have targeted several other women as well through similar modus operandi, the agency said, urging other victims to come forward and report their complaints, assuring them of complete confidentiality.

The public was advised to exercise caution while using matrimonial apps and social media platforms.

Man found shot dead

A young man with an alleged criminal record was found shot dead in North Karachi on Friday, police and rescue services officials said.

They said the body, bearing a gunshot wound, was found on the main road near Rehmania Mor in Sector 5B-3.

Khwaja Ajmer Nagri SHO Farrukh Hashmi said the deceased was identified as Sameer Masih, 30, a resident of Taiser Town.

He said initial investigations suggested that the deceased was travelling on a motorcycle as a pillion rider when he fell at the spot, while the other rider escaped. Sameer had a bullet wound to his back and was taken to Abbasi Shaheed Hospital, where doctors pronounced him dead.

The officer said the deceased had a criminal record, with five FIRs registered against him at different police stations.

He said it was possible that Sameer had been shot and wounded by a citizen during an attempted robbery somewhere in Manghopir, after which his accomplice abandoned him at the spot.

Man killed as coach overturns

A man was killed while five others were injured when a passenger coach overturned while avoiding a collision with a police mobile near Naval Colony gate in Baldia Town on Friday, police and rescue services officials said.

A traffic police official said that the passenger van was on its way from Hub Chowki to Karachi when it went out of control of its driver while avoiding an accident with a police mobile on the main Hub River Road.

headline: Oman rescues 25 from burning ship, Iran halts tankers
description: Oman said it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack, as Iran reported three oil tankers...
article_text:
Oman said it had rescued 25 sailors from a merchant ship set ablaze in an attack, as Iran reported three oil tankers were halted while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, reports AFP.

Muscat’s navy “carried out an evacuation operation for 25 crew members of the merchant ship RITI, flying the Panamanian flag, after it was targeted, which led to a fire breaking out on board,” Oman’s Maritime Security Centre said in a statement.

The crew members were provided with medical care, the Omani statement said, without giving details.

The Marine Traffic ship-tracking website described the RITI as a crude oil tanker.

headline: Man sets himself ablaze outside court after daughter’s ‘rapist’ acquitted in Lahore
description: A court acquitted the rape case accused on Thursday for lack of evidence, nine years after the case was institute.
author: The Newspaper's Staff Reporter
article_text:
LAHORE: A man set himself on fire outside the Muzaffargarh district courts on Friday, after an accused in the rape case of his daughter was acquitted after nine years of proceedings.

Identified as Allah Bakhshaya, the litigant poured petrol and set himself ablaze, following the acquittal of the accused.

He was shifted to the district headquarters hospital in critical condition, where doctors said he suffered 45.5pc burns, Rescue 1122 says.

A court acquitted the rape case accused on Thursday for lack of evidence, nine years after the case was instituted.

The litigant said he had spent years pursuing the case and that his daughter had also been divorced by her husband because of rape.

Published in Dawn, October 31st, 2026
