headline: UK PM 'open' to slavery apology but not reparations
description: "I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age," Andy Burnham says.
author: AFP
article_text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday he was “open” to the UK issuing a formal apology for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations.

The Labour leader made the remarks days before attending a Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua and Barbuda, as King Charles III tours the Caribbean.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnam wrote in The Guardian newspaper.

The transatlantic slave trade was a “brutal and barbaric violation” of the rights of those enslaved, he said, adding that his government wanted a “structured dialogue with those affected”.

“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”

The king is due to address the Commonwealth summit, which runs from November 1 to 4. Britain’s central role in slavery and the treatment of people in its former colonies has loomed over the 77-year-old monarch’s Caribbean tour.

In the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” during the first leg of his visit.

The UK has never formally apologised for slavery nor or agreed to pay reparations.

Burnham again rejected financial compensation, writing: “I do not believe that is the right answer.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Britain profited for centuries from colonialism and the slave trade. In 1833, parliament passed a law to abolish slavery.

“I want to express my sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering of so many millions and to recognise the way it still shapes our world today,” Burnam wrote in The Guardian newspaper.

The transatlantic slave trade was a “brutal and barbaric violation” of the rights of those enslaved, he said, adding that his government wanted a “structured dialogue with those affected”.

“Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”

The king is due to address the Commonwealth summit, which runs from November 1 to 4. Britain’s central role in slavery and the treatment of people in its former colonies has loomed over the 77-year-old monarch’s Caribbean tour.

In the Bahamas on Tuesday, Charles acknowledged “the great suffering of the past” during the first leg of his visit.

The UK has never formally apologised for slavery nor or agreed to pay reparations.

Burnham again rejected financial compensation, writing: “I do not believe that is the right answer.

“I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part.”

Britain profited for centuries from colonialism and the slave trade. In 1833, parliament passed a law to abolish slavery.

headline: Iran says fishermen found after accusing US of attack in Hormuz

article_text:
Iran says two fishermen it had reported missing have now been found, following what it called a US attack on a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, AFP reports.

“Two fishermen from Qeshm, who had gone missing following an attack by the American enemy on their fishing boat this morning, have been found,” state television says.

Earlier, state TV cited a provincial official as saying that two fishermen had gone missing and two others were wounded in what he called an attack by the United States on their vessel in the crucial Hormuz waterway.

AFP has contacted US Central Command (Centcom), which oversees American military operations in the region, for comment.

headline: Pakistan’s Punjab records 4.2 times more crop-fire detections than Indian Punjab: report
description: Between October 1 and 29, Okara recorded the highest number of fire spots, at 2,144, followed by Gujranwala with 1,011 and Nankana Sahib with 1,003.
author: Imran Gabol
article_text:
LAHORE: Crop-fire detections in Pakistan’s Punjab were 4.2 times higher than in Indian Punjab during the first 29 days of October, according to satellite data, as the province grapples with worsening smog.

According to an analysis published by environmental monitoring website HamariHawa, Nasa satellites detected 13,241 fire spots in Pakistan’s Punjab between Oct 1 and 29, compared with 3,158 in Indian Punjab — 4.2 times as many detections.

The report, based on data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), collected through VIIRS instruments aboard the Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 satellites, found that 92 per cent of the detected fire spots in Pakistan’s Punjab were located on farmland and were likely associated with crop burning.

The analysis also found that 6,655 fire spots, around half of the monthly total, were detected during the last seven days of October, indicating an increase in burning activity. Oct 29 was the busiest day, with 1,327 fire spots recorded in Pakistan’s Punjab.

A comparison based solely on data from the Suomi NPP satellite, which provides a consistent basis for examining trends over different years, showed that 4,562 fire spots were detected in Pakistan’s Punjab, compared with 918 in Indian Punjab, between Oct 1 and 29.

The findings mark a reversal of the situation in 2019, when Indian Punjab recorded almost five times as many fire detections as Pakistan’s Punjab during the same period, with 14,002 compared with 2,908.

HamariHawa’s historical analysis showed that Indian Punjab reduced its satellite-detected crop fires by 95 per cent between 2021 and 2025, while detections in Pakistan’s Punjab increased by 33 per cent between 2019 and 2025. In 2025, Pakistan’s Punjab recorded 12,364 fire spots, compared with 3,714 in Indian Punjab — 3.3 times as many.

The latest data showed that agricultural burning in Pakistan’s Punjab was concentrated in the rice-growing belt around Lahore. Okara recorded the highest number of fire spots, at 2,144, followed by Gujranwala with 1,011 and Nankana Sahib with 1,003 between Oct 1 and 29.

The three districts collectively recorded 4,158 fire spots, exceeding the total of 3,158 detections recorded across Indian Punjab during the same period.

Pakpattan recorded 922 fire spots, followed by Sheikhupura with 756, Hafizabad with 713, Dera Ghazi Khan with 710, Kasur with 699, Khanewal with 682 and Jhang with 676.

The report noted that these districts lie around Lahore, meaning smoke from agricultural fires across different parts of the province could contribute to the city’s deteriorating air quality, depending on wind direction.

However, the website cautioned that satellite detections indicate locations where fires were burning when satellites passed overhead and do not measure the area burnt or the volume of smoke produced. Fires occurring between satellite passes, or those obscured by clouds and thick smoke, may also go undetected.

HamariHawa said it had used the same methodology on both sides of the border and cross-checked its figures for Indian Punjab against official Indian fire counts, finding a strong correlation between the two datasets. It also pointed out that Pakistan had no comparable publicly available official daily fire-count series.

The satellite findings come as the Punjab Environment Protection Agency (EPA) intensifies its pre-smog enforcement campaign across the province, combining action against brick kilns, industrial pollution, plastic burning and construction dust with measures to prevent agricultural fires.

According to official figures for Sept 28 to Oct 27, the agency inspected 11,580 brick kilns, demolished 197 non-compliant kilns, sealed 163 units and registered 162 cases. Fines amounting to Rs40.7 million were also imposed during the operation.

Industrial pollution was another target, with 6,650 industrial units inspected, 22 demolished and 191 sealed. Officials issued 333 smog notices, registered 15 cases and imposed fines totalling Rs28m.

The agency also conducted 6,064 inspections targeting plastic burning, sealed 152 sites and confiscated 45,100 kilogrammes of plastic. In a separate exercise to monitor the installation of suction hoods at industrial facilities, 4,204 units were inspected, of which 1,863 had installed the required equipment. A total of 333 non-compliant sites were sealed.

To control dust from construction activities, operations were conducted in 397 union councils, with mist sprinklers installed at 49 locations.

In agricultural areas, the Punjab government has deployed 67 Quick Response Units (QRUs) to identify and prevent crop-residue burning through satellite-based fire detection and field monitoring. The teams are tasked with reaching fire hotspots, extinguishing fires and taking action against those responsible.

The department has also deployed drones, special night squads and field teams to identify pollution sources and enforce environmental regulations. Anti-smog guns are being operated at selected locations across Lahore to suppress suspended dust particles.

Meanwhile, according to the live air quality ranking published by Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir, Lahore recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 232 at 1pm on Oct 31, placing it at the top of the list of the world’s major cities. The readings placed Lahore in the ‘very unhealthy’ category.

Director General Environment Abdullah Nayyar Sheikh said the department was implementing a zero-tolerance policy against pollution, with enforcement teams remaining active during the day and at night.

He said action through fines, registration of cases and sealing of premises would continue against those violating environmental laws.

The satellite findings, meanwhile, highlight the challenge of controlling agricultural fires, particularly in districts surrounding Lahore, as the province enters the period when crop-residue burning and other pollution sources can combine to aggravate winter smog.

The findings mark a reversal of the situation in 2019, when Indian Punjab recorded almost five times as many fire detections as Pakistan’s Punjab during the same period, with 14,002 compared with 2,908.

In 2025, Pakistan’s Punjab recorded 12,364 fire spots, compared with 3,714 in Indian Punjab — 3.3 times as many.

The latest data showed that agricultural burning in Pakistan’s Punjab was concentrated in the rice-growing belt around Lahore. Okara recorded the highest number of fire spots, at 2,144, followed by Gujranwala with 1,011 and Nankana Sahib with 1,003 between Oct 1 and 29.

The three districts collectively recorded 4,158 fire spots, exceeding the total of 3,158 detections recorded across Indian Punjab during the same period.

Pakpattan recorded 922 fire spots, followed by Sheikhupura with 756, Hafizabad with 713, Dera Ghazi Khan with 710, Kasur with 699, Khanewal with 682 and Jhang with 676.

The report noted that these districts lie around Lahore, meaning smoke from agricultural fires across different parts of the province could contribute to the city’s deteriorating air quality, depending on wind direction.

However, the website cautioned that satellite detections indicate locations where fires were burning when satellites passed overhead and do not measure the area burnt or the volume of smoke produced. Fires occurring between satellite passes, or those obscured by clouds and thick smoke, may also go undetected.

HamariHawa said it had used the same methodology on both sides of the border and cross-checked its figures for Indian Punjab against official Indian fire counts, finding a strong correlation between the two datasets. It also pointed out that Pakistan had no comparable publicly available official daily fire-count series.

The satellite findings come as the Punjab Environment Protection Agency (EPA) intensifies its pre-smog enforcement campaign across the province, combining action against brick kilns, industrial pollution, plastic burning and construction dust with measures to prevent agricultural fires.

According to official figures for Sept 28 to Oct 27, the agency inspected 11,580 brick kilns, demolished 197 non-compliant kilns, sealed 163 units and registered 162 cases. Fines amounting to Rs40.7 million were also imposed during the operation.

Industrial pollution was another target, with 6,650 industrial units inspected, 22 demolished and 191 sealed. Officials issued 333 smog notices, registered 15 cases and imposed fines totalling Rs28m.

The agency also conducted 6,064 inspections targeting plastic burning, sealed 152 sites and confiscated 45,100 kilogrammes of plastic. In a separate exercise to monitor the installation of suction hoods at industrial facilities, 4,204 units were inspected, of which 1,863 had installed the required equipment. A total of 333 non-compliant sites were sealed.

To control dust from construction activities, operations were conducted in 397 union councils, with mist sprinklers installed at 49 locations.

In agricultural areas, the Punjab government has deployed 67 Quick Response Units (QRUs) to identify and prevent crop-residue burning through satellite-based fire detection and field monitoring. The teams are tasked with reaching fire hotspots, extinguishing fires and taking action against those responsible.

The department has also deployed drones, special night squads and field teams to identify pollution sources and enforce environmental regulations. Anti-smog guns are being operated at selected locations across Lahore to suppress suspended dust particles.

Meanwhile, according to the live air quality ranking published by Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir, Lahore recorded an Air Quality Index (AQI) of 232 at 1pm on Oct 31, placing it at the top of the list of the world’s major cities. The readings placed Lahore in the ‘very unhealthy’ category.

Director General Environment Abdullah Nayyar Sheikh said the department was implementing a zero-tolerance policy against pollution, with enforcement teams remaining active during the day and at night.

He said action through fines, registration of cases and sealing of premises would continue against those violating environmental laws.

The satellite findings, meanwhile, highlight the challenge of controlling agricultural fires, particularly in districts surrounding Lahore, as the province enters the period when crop-residue burning and other pollution sources can combine to aggravate winter smog.

headline: Syria weighing whether to join Makkah pact: foreign minister
description: Asaad al-Shaibani condemns attacks on Gulf states, denounces repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory.
author: AFP, News Desk
article_text:
Syria’s Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani on Saturday said Damascus was considering whether to join the Makkah defence pact that binds Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye.

The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement, signed on Aug 7, empowers the three members to consider an armed attack on one member an attack on all.

“Discussions are currently underway to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Makkah alliance,” Al Shaibani said at the Manama Dialogue conference in Bahrain.

According to Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA), speaking about the ongoing regional conflicts, the foreign minister expressed Damascus’s support for the Gulf states against any aggression and condemned missile and drone attacks.

“Geography is destiny, and integration is a choice. We have chosen to make our territory a bridge for prosperity and the exchange of interests, and we stand as a bulwark against turning Syria into a platform for threatening neighbouring countries,” he was quoted as saying.

Al Shaibani also condemned repeated Israeli attacks on Syrian territory, affirmed that occupied Golan was Syrian land, and called for a path to an independent Palestinian state.

Saudi Arabia has been rallying support against escalating attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, including a deadly strike that closed Riyadh’s international airport for two weeks this month.

Islamabad has two defence pacts with Riyadh aimed at collective deterrence — the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement between the two and the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement that also includes Turkiye.

Pakistan is providing “whatever support is needed” to defend Saudi Arabia amid the Houthi attacks, the military’s spokesperson Lieutenant General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said earlier this month.

However, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) director general also clarified that all members of the Makkah Defence Alliance were “absolutely clear […] that this alliance has no offensive intent; it is purely defensive”.

A day earlier, he said that the wording of the pact did not bar new members after being asked about whether Iran could join the agreement.

“Anyone who has a shared vision of collective deterrence and regional peace, why not? Everyone is most welcome,” he said, adding that it was for the political leadership of the three principal parties to decide.

In August, two weeks after the Makkah pact was signed, the Syrian foreign minister visited Pakistan and called on Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir.

They both discussed “regional security environment and avenues for enhanced bilateral defence and security cooperation”, ISPR said.

Amid the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, French President Emmanuel Macron made a surprise visit to Riyadh earlier this month and said France had sent troops to help shield a key Saudi oil terminal from attacks.

Also in October, the United Kingdom’s government announced it would deploy British fighter planes to help Saudi Arabia against the attacks.

headline: Yemen’s foreign minister describes Houthi siege of Taiz as a war crime
description: Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah Al-Zuba has described the Houthis’ siege of Taiz as a war crime, in which the...
article_text:
Yemeni Foreign Minister Afrah Al-Zuba has described the Houthis’ siege of Taiz as a war crime, in which the population’s need for food, medicine and fuel is being used as a tool for political pressure and blackmail, Al Jazeera reports, citing Yemeni state media Saba News Agency.

Al-Zuba, who is Yemen’s first female foreign minister, demanded the immediate lifting of the siege and the permanent and safe opening of roads in and out of the city.

Speaking at the third plenary session of the Manama Dialogue 2026 in Bahrain, the minister said that ending the Houthis’ attempted “coup” and restoring Yemeni state institutions is a shared responsibility between the countries of the Gulf Cooperation Council.

“The repercussions of the coup against the state have extended beyond Yemen’s borders, affecting the security of neighbouring countries, navigation, and international interests,” the minister was quoted as saying. “This necessitates translating solidarity into practical steps to address the source of threats and to establish sustainable stability.”

headline: Iran's supreme leader warns US, Israel of 'unrestricted geographical response' to new attacks
description: Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei orders commanders to update Iran's target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist enemy”.
author: AFP
article_text:
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday warned the United States and Israel against returning to war, according to a written statement, following threats from the Islamic republic’s foes of a possible resumption of strikes.

“If the enemies once again launch military or terrorist attacks, it is the armed forces of the Islamic Republic and the Iranian nation that will determine the time and conditions for ending them,” said a statement attributed to Khamenei posted on his website.

The remarks came during a reported meeting between Khamenei and senior military commanders, including armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi, army chief Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards commander Ahmad Vahidi. It was the first reported meeting between them.

Khamenei has not been publicly seen since he became supreme leader, following his father Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s assassination in US-Israeli strikes at the start of the Middle East war in February.

According to the statement, Khamenei ordered the commanders to ensure that “any level or type of threat must be met with an immediate, impactful and geographically unrestricted response”.

It also said that Khamenei ordered the commanders to update Iran’s target list to include “all types of tangible and intangible assets belonging to the American-Zionist (Israeli) enemy”.

The war began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, which swiftly responded with attacks on countries around the region.

The supreme leader’s statement came as fresh diplomatic efforts were under way to avert a resumption of fighting.

A Qatari delegation arrived in Tehran on Friday for talks with Iranian officials, after Iran reportedly received a letter from US Vice President JD Vance. According to Iranian media, Tehran had yet to respond to the letter.

headline: In the rent-a-loan business, you can pay but you can never leave
description: How private moneylenders trap the poor
author: Zareef Rind
article_text:
Alamgeer Khan appears in a white shalwar kameez with a waistcoat at Quetta Chai Cafe near Jamali Pul in Ayub Goth. He parks his motorcycle and takes his spot. The waiter brings the usual: green tea with ginger. Alamgeer makes a few entries in small diaries and a few phone calls. After the cup is drained, he starts on the roster of visits. They are rarely pleasant.

The fifty-five-year-old would rather euphemistically introduce himself as a businessman involved in financing than the less elegant ‘moneylender’. The business model is simple: the money is the product. People need it, he provides it, and he earns by charging for its use, a return on the capital he has invested. A less charitable definition is usury.

“Banks do the same thing,” he says, “but they write ‘Islamic’ in front so their work is considered halal, while ours, because we are uneducated commoners of society, is called usury, haram.”

He believes men like him are doing society and the government a favour by providing a service because banks aren’t doing their job. How is a daily wage plumber supposed to rustle up a Grade 10 government officer as a guarantor or provide gold or a credit history as a guarantee? Or a housewife? Would chickens work? Banks just don’t accept the kind of surety the plebs have. And what do the poor have in this society anyway? Except pain? If you could fill in details of your track record of survival for a Guzara Scheme, that might work.

Men like Alamgeer meet a need and earn a little money from doing so, but what is their recompense? “My money isn’t laying eggs in a box,” he adds, leaning heavily on a blunt idiom. It loses value to inflation. “We put it to use so that its value remains equal.”

What Alamgeer is failing to mention is that his ‘business’ of ‘financing’ is actually renting his money out. It locks the borrower in because the principal never gets paid.

The desperate office workerSimon is still living with the psychological scars from being locked in the jaws of a loan shark. The office helper at a large private sector organisation makes Rs46,000 as a salary. He lived with his parents, six siblings and then his wife and children in a katchi abadi with an uncle’s family. When a family dispute turned nasty, they decided to split from the uncle’s family and move out. His father’s work had dried up and not all of the siblings were earning steadily. So money was already tight.

When the cost of living crept up, he began to struggle with household expenses, and covering needs for his wife and child, and contributions in a joint family. At one point he thought a bank loan might be a safer option to tide him over but after a review of his documents, salary and family circumstances, it turned him down. When he did the math, it didn’t make sense anyway. The amount he had asked for would have to be repaid over two years, but the monthly repayment was higher than his salary.

An acquaintance introduced Simon to a ‘lender’ who gave him Rs50,000, which he had to repay at a monthly interest rate of 10pc or Rs5,000. The agreement was that the first month’s Rs5,000 interest was deducted upfront and so, although the loan was for Rs50,000, Simon took home Rs45,000 in cash.

After that, he had to pay Rs5,000 every month. “The lender was surprised because I paid him back promptly every month because my salary would come on time,” Simon says. “He said he had never had a client who paid before the end of the month.” The lender usually had to go bang on doors after the 15th to demand payments amid a lot of unpleasantness. This goodwill with Simon was rewarded as a five-hundred-rupee reduction, so the monthly repayment sank to Rs4,500.

This continued for a year. By the end of those 12 months, he had paid Rs60,000 in interest alone, while the principal amount of Rs50,000 remained undented. “The Rs50,000 is blocked,” Simon explains. “Unless you return the full amount in one go, the loan is not forgiven.” By this rationale, a borrower isn’t paying ‘interest’ but ‘rent’ on having borrowed a lump sum.

Meanwhile, he went further into debt for his sister’s, and later his brother’s weddings, so his principal ballooned to Rs500,000. This took his monthly rental payments to Rs50,000 at 10%. To make matters worse, he was unable to pay at all for three months in the middle. That unpaid Rs135,000 was added to the principal, increasing his debt to Rs635,000. Now, at the new 10pc rental, he had to cough up Rs63,500 a month. That was more than his salary. “Every month when it hit the 20th, I would start going crazy,” he says. He couldn’t sleep for the stress that he’d have to make the payments. “I went out of control,” he says, describing himself mentally and behaviourally.

At work, he began eating into his health insurance by making increasingly frequent trips to the ER. His diabetes was out of control and the doctors said it was stress. Then his heart started to waver. “I was in serious trouble,” he says. There was little room for him to simply walk away. The lender had kept signed cheques as security, along with his employment records, home address and the agreement. “If I gave him a hard time, he could always just try to cash a check I’d given him for Rs200,000 and it would bounce. Then there’s an FIR. This is how they’d drag you through the mud.” The threat of the lender turning up at his workplace and making “drama” was enough to keep landing Simon in the ER.

Eventually, Simon received help from someone to clear the Rs635,000 debt in one fell swoop. It was only then that the register was crossed out.

The law, in principle

Pakistan has a difficult relationship with usury. The Constitution says it should be abolished, and more recently the Federal Shariat Court said the country had to go interest-free by the end of 2027. But it still works in banks and is legal for now.

All the provinces have taken a hard line against the kind of predatory financial schemes Simon was ensnared in. They all ban private money lending on interest and attach punishments and fines, but enforcement is fraught.

Clever bargains

Rent-a-loan methods are perhaps the most damning financial schemes. Others are more creative in their use of compounding interest and methods of using frontmen.

Ustaad Ghulam Khan tells the story of how he was ensnared almost 20 years ago, when he needed Rs100,000. He went to an acquaintance who ran a tyre shop but was known to lend money, even though he maintained a pretense around it. The shop owner said he would not give Ghulam Khan the cash directly, but truck tyres worth Rs100,000 instead.

The shopkeeper then introduced Ghulam Khan to a man sitting at the shop, who he said was his ‘cousin’ who would buy the tyres.

Thus, Ghulam Khan ‘bought’ the tyres on credit for Rs100,000 and immediately ‘sold’ them to the other man for Rs90,000 in cash. The tyres never moved from the shop.

The rule was that he had to return the full Rs100,000 within a month. If he failed, he would have to pay 25 pc interest every month while the original principal remained outstanding. Needless to say, he never managed.

That was the first time the lender made him sign a stamp paper, says Ghulam Khan. People close to the lender were brought in as witnesses, and the agreement stated that whenever Ghulam Khan failed to pay the interest for a particular month, the unpaid interest would be added to the principal and the following month’s interest would be calculated on the increased amount. In this case too, if payments were skipped some months, they would compound.

He struggled to pay for over three years and watched the original amount swell to Rs600,000, with monthly payments hitting Rs150,000. “How I managed to arrange that money is known only to me and my Allah,” he says. “I did all kinds of good and bad things just to keep paying the interest.”

Whenever he missed a payment, the lender would come to his house and bang loudly on the door so the neighbors could hear that he owed him money. Going to the police was out of the question because he feared the man had connections.

The lender would offer him new loans, sometimes in goods and sometimes in cash, to pay off old ones. The old account would be closed and a new account with a new interest burden would begin.

Eventually, Ghulam Khan sold ancestral land, grew indebted to his own brothers and sisters and used that money to set himself free. But by then, his life had been shattered.

“To this day, I have never been able to stand on my own feet again,” he says.

In kind

The lending business has moved beyond cash, say people familiar with the market. Money lenders have branched into electronics and the auto sector. They provide televisions, refrigerators, washing machines and other goods on installments. Motorcycles and cars are given on credit, often at higher prices.

This is how it works: according to one market expert, some goods sold on installments are priced 30pc higher than if you paid cash. The lender orders lower-priced products from companies, and recovers the cost through the down payment and early instalments, and treating the remaining instalments as their interest-based profit.

Rajab Khan explains the car financing business he got into in 2018-19. He started with one car, paid half its price, and was given one year to pay the rest. After using the car for some time, he sold it at a profit, giving that buyer a year to make the remaining payment. He then bought another car and continued doing the same thing.

For a while, the business worked. But after 2020 or 2021, car prices skyrocketed. Customers who had managed to pay a down payment of half the price could no longer do so. Then Rajab was introduced to Shah-ji, a car showroom owner off Khalid Bin Waleed Road in Karachi. Shah-ji offered cars at much lower down payments, sometimes as little as 10 per cent. Customers could get cars without arranging half the price upfront, and Rajab saw an opportunity to continue with his business.

The problem began when one customer failed to pay the Rs6 million that remained outstanding on a car worth Rs12.5m. Rajab told the customer that he had two choices: either have the car auctioned or pay an additional Rs500,000 for another month. The customer agreed, while Shah-ji took a cheque from Rajab as a guarantee.

When the customer again failed to pay the Rs6m the following month, Rajab had to pay the Rs500,000 himself. The same thing happened again, and the additional amount kept accumulating. The original Rs6m, he says, eventually reached Rs15m.

Shah-ji was holding on to the files that Rajab had arranged for other customers so he began repossessing those cars, even in cases where their owners had been paying installments. Because one party had failed to return the outstanding amount, the cars of other customers were also being taken back.

Rajab was trapped from both sides. The people whose cars had been repossessed were demanding that he return their money or get their cars back, while Shah-ji continued increasing the amount he owed.

Rajab grew bankrupt, reduced to unsuccessfully pleading with Shah-ji for mercy and offering to recover the amounts or repossess the cars. As he feared, the next stops were the police stations and courts over the bounced blank checks. He secured pre-arrest bail and appeared on June 16, 2026 before the Karachi City Court, expecting the matter to proceed through the legal system.

However, as he came out of court, police officers stopped him and took him away in a private vehicle. He describes what followed as an arrest that felt like an abduction. Instead of being taken directly to a police station, he was allegedly driven around the city for eight hours, with the complainant accompanying the police. He says he was pressured to sign new cheques and when he refused, he was eventually taken to a police station in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, where another FIR was registered against him.

He was sent to judicial custody. When he secured bail in the new FIR, his arrest was shown in yet another case. He eventually spent 17 days in jail before securing bail in all three FIRs.

By then, the cases had begun to take on a character that Rajab found difficult to understand. One vehicle dispute, he says, had resulted in FIRs at two different police stations in Karachi. In another FIR registered in Thatta, he was accused of buying a buffalo but failing to pay for it. “They have my cheques. By using their influence, they are making up all kinds of cases against me from wherever they can,” Rajab says.

Under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, a dishonoured cheque issued dishonestly towards repayment of a loan or fulfilment of an obligation can lead to criminal proceedings. In such a case, the person holding the cheque can become the complainant and the person who issued it can face an FIR as the accused. Thus, while Rajab describes himself as the victim of a lending arrangement, the legal process can place the showroom owner, who holds his cheques, on the other side of the case.

Rajab approached the Sindh High Court through his lawyer, arguing that the same underlying dispute was being presented in different forms through different FIRs. He asked the court to have all the cases brought on record and to stop what he described as the registration of further false cases. According to him, the police have neither provided a complete list of the FIRs against him nor stopped the registration of new cases. At present, there are eight FIRs against him at different police stations in Karachi and Thatta. He has secured bail in them and is waiting for the cases to proceed, but remains afraid that he could be arrested again whenever he appears for a hearing.

Two sides of a coin

As anyone will tell you, getting a loan from a bank is one of the hardest financial moves to pull. You need a valid CNIC, a steady job and salary slips, in fact a minimum salary. It is small wonder, then, that the State Bank’s own figures show banks lending far more to the government than to people. In the first half of this year, 79.4pc of the growth in banks’ assets came from investments, almost all in government securities. Loans made up just 8.7pc. Men like Ghulam Khan were never in line, and men like Alamgeer can sneer at the system that doesn’t cater to the poor.

“When there were no banks, people like us were the ones running this entire system,” Alamgeer says. But now banks have the protection of the state and the law, while small financiers like him are on their own. “Universities, schools, colleges, even madrasas defend the banking system, while we are made to appear as devils in all this.”

Ghulam Khan spent over three years trying to keep up with his payments before selling land. Simon needed someone to bail him out. Rajab remains in court over the consequences of a car-financing arrangement.

Meanwhile, at around 7am each day, Alamgeer will return to Quetta Chai Café. The waiter will bring his green tea with ginger. He will take the small diaries from his waistcoat and begin going through the accounts before setting out for his rounds.

Note: All names have been changed to protect victims.

Alamgeer Khan appears in a white shalwar kameez with a waistcoat at Quetta Chai Cafe near Jamali Pul in Ayub Goth. He parks his motorcycle and takes his spot. The waiter brings the usual: green tea with ginger. Alamgeer makes a few entries in small diaries and a few phone calls. After the cup is drained, he starts on the roster of visits. They are rarely pleasant.

The fifty-five-year-old would rather euphemistically introduce himself as a businessman involved in financing than the less elegant ‘moneylender’. The business model is simple: the money is the product. People need it, he provides it, and he earns by charging for its use, a return on the capital he has invested. A less charitable definition is usury.

“Banks do the same thing,” he says, “but they write ‘Islamic’ in front so their work is considered halal, while ours, because we are uneducated commoners of society, is called usury, haram.”

He believes men like him are doing society and the government a favour by providing a service because banks aren’t doing their job. How is a daily wage plumber supposed to rustle up a Grade 10 government officer as a guarantor or provide gold or a credit history as a guarantee? Or a housewife? Would chickens work? Banks just don’t accept the kind of surety the plebs have. And what do the poor have in this society anyway? Except pain? If you could fill in details of your track record of survival for a Guzara Scheme, that might work.

Men like Alamgeer meet a need and earn a little money from doing so, but what is their recompense? “My money isn’t laying eggs in a box,” he adds, leaning heavily on a blunt idiom. It loses value to inflation. “We put it to use so that its value remains equal.”

What Alamgeer is failing to mention is that his ‘business’ of ‘financing’ is actually renting his money out. It locks the borrower in because the principal never gets paid.

The desperate office worker
Simon is still living with the psychological scars from being locked in the jaws of a loan shark. The office helper at a large private sector organisation makes Rs46,000 as a salary. He lived with his parents, six siblings and then his wife and children in a katchi abadi with an uncle’s family. When a family dispute turned nasty, they decided to split from the uncle’s family and move out. His father’s work had dried up and not all of the siblings were earning steadily. So money was already tight.

When the cost of living crept up, he began to struggle with household expenses, and covering needs for his wife and child, and contributions in a joint family. At one point he thought a bank loan might be a safer option to tide him over but after a review of his documents, salary and family circumstances, it turned him down. When he did the math, it didn’t make sense anyway. The amount he had asked for would have to be repaid over two years, but the monthly repayment was higher than his salary.

An acquaintance introduced Simon to a ‘lender’ who gave him Rs50,000, which he had to repay at a monthly interest rate of 10pc or Rs5,000. The agreement was that the first month’s Rs5,000 interest was deducted upfront and so, although the loan was for Rs50,000, Simon took home Rs45,000 in cash.

This goodwill with Simon was rewarded as a five-hundred-rupee reduction, so the monthly repayment sank to Rs4,500.

This continued for a year. By the end of those 12 months, he had paid Rs60,000 in interest alone, while the principal amount of Rs50,000 remained undented. “The Rs50,000 is blocked,” Simon explains. “Unless you return the full amount in one go, the loan is not forgiven.” By this rationale, a borrower isn’t paying ‘interest’ but ‘rent’ on having borrowed a lump sum.

Meanwhile, he went further into debt for his sister’s, and later his brother’s weddings, so his principal ballooned to Rs500,000. This took his monthly rental payments to Rs50,000 at 10%. To make matters worse, he was unable to pay at all for three months in the middle. That unpaid Rs135,000 was added to the principal, increasing his debt to Rs635,000. Now, at the new 10pc rental, he had to cough up Rs63,500 a month. That was more than his salary. “Every month when it hit the 20th, I would start going crazy,” he says. He couldn’t sleep for the stress that he’d have to make the payments. “I went out of control,” he says, describing himself mentally and behaviourally.

At work, he began eating into his health insurance by making increasingly frequent trips to the ER. His diabetes was out of control and the doctors said it was stress. Then his heart started to waver. “I was in serious trouble,” he says. There was little room for him to simply walk away. The lender had kept signed cheques as security, along with his employment records, home address and the agreement. “If I gave him a hard time, he could always just try to cash a check I’d given him for Rs200,000 and it would bounce. Then there’s an FIR. This is how they’d drag you through the mud.” The threat of the lender turning up at his workplace and making “drama” was enough to keep landing Simon in the ER.

Eventually, Simon received help from someone to clear the Rs635,000 debt in one fell swoop. It was only then that the register was crossed out.

Pakistan has a difficult relationship with usury. The Constitution says it should be abolished, and more recently the Federal Shariat Court said the country had to go interest-free by the end of 2027. But it still works in banks and is legal for now.

All the provinces have taken a hard line against the kind of predatory financial schemes Simon was ensnared in. They all ban private money lending on interest and attach punishments and fines, but enforcement is fraught.

He went to an acquaintance who ran a tyre shop but was known to lend money, even though he maintained a pretense around it. The shop owner said he would not give Ghulam Khan the cash directly, but truck tyres worth Rs100,000 instead.

The shopkeeper then introduced Ghulam Khan to a man sitting at the shop, who he said was his ‘cousin’ who would buy the tyres.

Thus, Ghulam Khan ‘bought’ the tyres on credit for Rs100,000 and immediately ‘sold’ them to the other man for Rs90,000 in cash. The tyres never moved from the shop.

The rule was that he had to return the full Rs100,000 within a month. If he failed, he would have to pay 25 pc interest every month while the original principal remained outstanding. Needless to say, he never managed.

That was the first time the lender made him sign a stamp paper, says Ghulam Khan. However, as he came out of court, police officers stopped him and took him away in a private vehicle. He describes what followed as an arrest that felt like an abduction. Instead of being taken directly to a police station, he was allegedly driven around the city for eight hours, with the complainant accompanying the police. Shah-ji was holding on to the files that Rajab had arranged for other customers so he began repossessing those cars, even in cases where their owners had been paying installments. Because one party had failed to return the outstanding amount, the cars of other customers were also being taken back.
Rajab was trapped from both sides. The people whose cars had been repossessed were demanding that he return their money or get their cars back, while Shah-ji continued increasing the amount he owed.

Rajab grew bankrupt, reduced to unsuccessfully pleading with Shah-ji for mercy and offering to recover the amounts or repossess the cars. As he feared, the next stops were the police stations and courts over the bounced blank checks. He secured pre-arrest bail and appeared on June 16, 2026 before the Karachi City Court, expecting the matter to proceed through the legal system.

However, as he came out of court, police officers stopped him and took him away in a private vehicle. He describes what followed as an arrest that felt like an abduction. Instead of being taken directly to a police station, he was allegedly driven around the city for eight hours, with the complainant accompanying the police. He says he was pressured to sign new cheques and when he refused, he was eventually taken to a police station in Gulshan-e-Iqbal, where another FIR was registered against him.
He was sent to judicial custody. When he secured bail in the new FIR, his arrest was shown in yet another case. He eventually spent 17 days in jail before securing bail in all three FIRs.

By then, the cases had begun to take on a character that Rajab found difficult to understand. One vehicle dispute, he says, had resulted in FIRs at two different police stations in Karachi. In another FIR registered in Thatta, he was accused of buying a buffalo but failing to pay for it. “They have my cheques. By using their influence, they are making up all kinds of cases against me from wherever they can,” Rajab says.

Under Section 489-F of the Pakistan Penal Code, a dishonoured cheque issued dishonestly towards repayment of a loan or fulfilment of an obligation can lead to criminal proceedings. In such a case, the person holding the cheque can become the complainant and the person who issued it can face an FIR as the accused. Thus, while Rajab describes himself as the victim of a lending arrangement, the legal process can place the showroom owner, who holds his cheques, on the other side of the case.

Rajab approached the Sindh High Court through his lawyer, arguing that the same underlying dispute was being presented in different forms through different FIRs. He asked the court to have all the cases brought on record and to stop what he described as the registration of further false cases. According to him, the police have neither provided a complete list of the FIRs against him nor stopped the registration of new cases. At present, there are eight FIRs against him at different police stations in Karachi and Thatta. He has secured bail in them and is waiting for the cases to proceed, but remains afraid that he could be arrested again whenever he appears for a hearing.
Two sides of a coin

As anyone will tell you, getting a loan from a bank is one of the hardest financial moves to pull. You need a valid CNIC, a steady job and salary slips, in fact a minimum salary. It is small wonder, then, that the State Bank’s own figures show banks lending far more to the government than to people. In the first half of this year, 79.4pc of the growth in banks’ assets came from investments, almost all in government securities. Loans made up just 8.7pc. Men like Ghulam Khan were never in line, and men like Alamgeer can sneer at the system that doesn’t cater to the poor.

“When there were no banks, people like us were the ones running this entire system,” Alamgeer says. But now banks have the protection of the state and the law, while small financiers like him are on their own. “Universities, schools, colleges, even madrasas defend the banking system, while we are made to appear as devils in all this.”

Ghulam Khan spent over three years trying to keep up with his payments before selling land. Simon needed someone to bail him out. Rajab remains in court over the consequences of a car-financing arrangement.

Meanwhile, at around 7am each day, Alamgeer will return to Quetta Chai Café. The waiter will bring his green tea with ginger. He will take the small diaries from his waistcoat and begin going through the accounts before setting out for his rounds.

headline: Iranian delegation arrives in Qatar amid reported breakthrough in talks with US: report

article_text:
An Iranian delegation, including a deputy to Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, is in Qatar for talks following a reported breakthrough in indirect negotiations between Tehran and Washington, Anadolu reports citing a Qatari newspaper.

Citing an Iranian source, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed reports that the delegation is in the Qatari capital, Doha, “to facilitate engagement with the Qatari mediator.”

The visit follows “intensive discussions held by a Qatari negotiating delegation in Tehran, which resulted in a breakthrough in indirect negotiations between Tehran and Washington,” the newspaper reports, citing the source.

The discussions have also paved the way for the Iranian negotiating team to accompany the Qatari delegation on its return trip to Doha, according to the report.

“Negotiations with the US side are taking place indirectly through the mediator, not directly,” the Iranian source tells the newspaper.

headline: AI-based attendance system leads to dismissal of 72 doctors in Balochistan
description: The total number of employees dismissed from the Health Department has now reached 200.
author: Saleem Shahid
article_text:
QUETTA: The Balochistan Health Department on Saturday dismissed 72 doctors from government service for prolonged absence from duty.

The doctors were dismissed under an artificial intelligence (AI)-based attendance system introduced by the provincial government to ensure that medical staff reported for duty regularly.

According to an official notification issued by the Balochistan health secretary, the action was taken under Section 4(B)(viii) of the Balochistan Employees’ Efficiency and Disciplinary Act (BEEDA), 2011.

The notification said the medical officers (BPS-17) and senior medical officers (BPS-18) had been dismissed from service with immediate effect on account of their unauthorised absence from government duty.

The dismissal orders were issued with immediate effect, according to the notification.

The total number of employees dismissed from the Health Department has now reached 200.

Health Department officials said Rs410 million had so far been deducted from employees’ salaries over absenteeism.

The notification added that notices had been issued to 11,000 employees, seeking explanations for violations of attendance and disciplinary rules.

“Departmental action is under way against another 800 employees,” it said.

In a statement, Balochistan Health Minister Bakht Muhammad Kakar said the doctors had repeatedly been issued notices directing them to report for duty, but they had failed to respond.

Their continued absence from duty and failure to respond to repeated notices had compelled the government to take action, he added.

“We have zero tolerance for absenteeism and negligence among medical staff and doctors in the performance of their official duties,” Kakar said, adding that the Health Department was making efforts to provide people with the best possible healthcare facilities at their doorsteps.

He said reforms were under way to improve the performance of the provincial Health Department on the instructions of Chief Minister Mir Sarfraz Bugti.

He added that staff attendance at government hospitals and health centres was being monitored through an AI-based attendance system.

headline: Saudi minister says efforts under way to prevent military escalation in US-Iran war
description: Saudi Arabia has said the region wants a return to peace, as concerns grow over a possible new escalation between...
article_text:
Saudi Arabia has said the region wants a return to peace, as concerns grow over a possible new escalation between the United States, Israel and Iran, Al Jazeera reports.

Speaking at a security forum in Bahrain on Saturday, Saudi Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Waleed ElKhereiji said efforts were under way to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the crisis with Iran.

“If you look at the efforts that everybody is trying to do, the message is very clear. People in this part of the world want to bring peace back to the region,” he was quoted as saying.

ElKhereiji added, however, that no one could predict the outcome of those efforts.

headline: Kamindu Mendis blitz sets Pakistan 326 to win in tri-series final
description: The left-hander’s commanding innings ensured Pakistan were set a target of 326 to claim the title.
author: Dawn Sport
article_text:
Kamindu Mendis struck a belligerent 131 off 128 balls, his maiden One-day International century, to help Sri Lanka post a formidable 325 against Pakistan in the tri-series final at Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore on Saturday.

The left-hander’s commanding innings ensured Pakistan were set a target of 326 to claim the title, after the Islanders recovered from a promising start by the hosts’ bowlers to build a strong platform before Pakistan pulled things back in the closing overs.

Sri Lanka openers Kamindu and Avishka Fernando began briskly, scoring freely while keeping risks to a minimum. Their assured start took the visitors to more than 50 without loss at the end of the first 10 overs.

Pakistan had brought in Faheem Ashraf for Shadab Khan, who was ruled out of the final on medical grounds after being struck by a bouncer in the fifth ODI against Sri Lanka. The visitors, meanwhile, replaced pacer Eshan Malinga with spinner Maheesh Theekshana. The contrasting selections suggested the two sides had read the conditions differently.

That assessment appeared to be reflected in the early stages of Sri Lanka’s innings. Pakistan’s pace attack struggled to make an impact, while it was Salman Ali Agha who provided the first breakthroughs, claiming the only two wickets the hosts took before the final 10 overs.

Avishka missed a sweep against Salman and was struck on the front pad, with the umpire raising his finger to give the opener out leg-before in the 18th over. Four overs later, Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis stepped out of his crease and drove the ball back towards Salman, who showed sharp reflexes to leap and take a superb return catch.

Beyond those two dismissals, the innings belonged largely to Kamindu, who took charge of the scoring and kept Sri Lanka moving through the middle overs.

He negotiated a brief period in which boundaries were hard to come by before shifting gears and taking on the Pakistan bowlers. At the other end, Pavan Rathnayake provided valuable support, the pair adding 146 runs for the third wicket after Rathnayake came in at number four.

Kamindu brought up his century in the 34th over, expertly cutting a Faheem delivery over the wicket-keeper’s head to reach the landmark. His innings combined patience with timely aggression, keeping the scoreboard ticking while ensuring Sri Lanka retained control.

Rathnayake continued the rich vein of form he has displayed throughout the series, bringing up another half-century in 47 deliveries. He used the pull and sweep shots effectively to put pressure on the bowlers and maintain the momentum of the partnership.

It was an underwhelming outing for Pakistan’s bowlers, with Arafat Minhas finishing wicketless and Naseem Shah conceding at an economy rate of eight runs per over. However, the fielding side managed to rein in Sri Lanka during the death overs and prevent the visitors from making a late charge towards a total of 350 or more.

At 238-2 after 40 overs, Sri Lanka appeared well placed to post a total close to, or in excess of, 350. But Pakistan struck back through their captain Shaheen Shah Afridi, who trapped Kamindu leg-before in the 42nd over before dismissing Dasun Shanaka soon afterwards. Shanaka had made a brisk 17 off just nine balls.

Rathnayake’s innings ended when he miscued a delivery from Haris Rauf and was caught by Babar Azam at wide long-on. Janith Liyanage also struggled to get going, scoring just six off nine balls before falling to Naseem.

Haris and Naseem then dismissed Dunith Wellalage and Sahan Arachchige in quick succession, further slowing Sri Lanka’s progress. However, a wayward penultimate over from Naseem allowed the visitors to cross the 320-run mark. Sri Lanka added four more runs to finish on 325, leaving Pakistan with a challenging target of 326 in their bid to lift the trophy.

article_html:
Kamindu Mendis struck a belligerent 131 off 128 balls, his maiden One-day International century, to help Sri Lanka post a formidable 325 against Pakistan in the tri-series final at Gaddafi Stadium in Lahore on Saturday.

The left-hander’s commanding innings ensured Pakistan were set a target of 326 to claim the title, after the Islanders recovered from a promising start by the hosts’ bowlers to build a strong platform before Pakistan pulled things back in the closing overs.

Sri Lanka openers Kamindu and Avishka Fernando began briskly, scoring freely while keeping risks to a minimum. Their assured start took the visitors to more than 50 without loss at the end of the first 10 overs.

Pakistan had brought in Faheem Ashraf for Shadab Khan, who was ruled out of the final on medical grounds after being struck by a bouncer in the fifth ODI against Sri Lanka. The visitors, meanwhile, replaced pacer Eshan Malinga with spinner Maheesh Theekshana. The contrasting selections suggested the two sides had read the conditions differently.

That assessment appeared to be reflected in the early stages of Sri Lanka’s innings. Pakistan’s pace attack struggled to make an impact, while it was Salman Ali Agha who provided the first breakthroughs, claiming the only two wickets the hosts took before the final 10 overs.

Avishka missed a sweep against Salman and was struck on the front pad, with the umpire raising his finger to give the opener out leg-before in the 18th over. Four overs later, Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis stepped out of his crease and drove the ball back towards Salman, who showed sharp reflexes to leap and take a superb return catch.

Beyond those two dismissals, the innings belonged largely to Kamindu, who took charge of the scoring and kept Sri Lanka moving through the middle overs.

He negotiated a brief period in which boundaries were hard to come by before shifting gears and taking on the Pakistan bowlers. At the other end, Pavan Rathnayake provided valuable support, the pair adding 146 runs for the third wicket after Rathnayake came in at number four.

Kamindu brought up his century in the 34th over, expertly cutting a Faheem delivery over the wicket-keeper’s head to reach the landmark. His innings combined patience with timely aggression, keeping the scoreboard ticking while ensuring Sri Lanka retained control.

Rathnayake continued the rich vein of form he has displayed throughout the series, bringing up another half-century in 47 deliveries. He used the pull and sweep shots effectively to put pressure on the bowlers and maintain the momentum of the partnership.

It was an underwhelming outing for Pakistan’s bowlers, with Arafat Minhas finishing wicketless and Naseem Shah conceding at an economy rate of eight runs per over. However, the fielding side managed to rein in Sri Lanka during the death overs and prevent the visitors from making a late charge towards a total of 350 or more.

At 238-2 after 40 overs, Sri Lanka appeared well placed to post a total close to, or in excess of, 350. But Pakistan struck back through their captain Shaheen Shah Afridi, who trapped Kamindu leg-before in the 42nd over before dismissing Dasun Shanaka soon afterwards. Shanaka had made a brisk 17 off just nine balls.

Rathnayake’s innings ended when he miscued a delivery from Haris Rauf and was caught by Babar Azam at wide long-on. Janith Liyanage also struggled to get going, scoring just six off nine balls before falling to Naseem.

Haris and Naseem then dismissed Dunith Wellalage and Sahan Arachchige in quick succession, further slowing Sri Lanka’s progress. However, a wayward penultimate over from Naseem allowed the visitors to cross the 320-run mark. Sri Lanka added four more runs to finish on 325, leaving Pakistan with a challenging target of 326 in their bid to lift the trophy.

headline: Crypto exchanges call for quick moves to bolster defences after Binance heist
description: Security experts say a common tactic of social engineering may have been involved in compromising a software engineer's laptop suspected to have led to the hack.
author: Reuters
article_text:
Crypto exchanges are taking quick action to bolster their defences and urging greater industry-wide information-sharing after a record $6.3 billion hack of Binance exposed their vulnerability just as they become more embedded in mainstream finance.

Coinbase said it made adjustments to its systems that store cryptocurrency keys offline “solely out of an abundance of caution”, while Kraken said it was monitoring industry incidents for lessons it could apply to its defences.

But the industry will need to move urgently, analysts and industry executives said, as United States President Donald Trump’s regulators promote deeper integration of digital assets into the financial system, raising the stakes for an industry with a history of big hacks.

“For crypto to reach its full potential, the security situation must be addressed immediately,” said Chris Perkins, Franklin Templeton’s head of crypto.

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, halted withdrawals after Thursday’s attack, which analysts blamed on North Korea and said it would use company funds to cover the losses.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X that the complex attack may have begun with a compromised software engineer’s laptop, giving hackers access to systems used to process withdrawals. The company later found additional breaches, while software designed to erase traces of the attack hampered the investigation.

Rival crypto exchanges moved quickly on Friday to shore up their own systems and to reassure customers that their tokens were safe. Full-time teams at Kraken look for potential vulnerabilities every day, a Kraken spokesperson said.

Still, even as the industry reeled from the biggest cryptocurrency heist of all time, executives expressed confidence that Binance had sufficient resources to cover the losses and that the hack would not have broader financial repercussions.

Bitcoin fell more than 4 per cent on Thursday while ether, the second-largest cryptocurrency, fell more than 5pc, although both tokens recovered some of that ground on Friday.

“Our expectation is the industry writ large will actually not suffer material losses, even though Binance is obviously going to have to deal with the exploit directly,” said Josh Riezman, chief legal and strategy officer at crypto firm GSR.

The bulk of the heist unfolded in around 20 minutes late on Thursday and bore similarities to previous attacks blamed on North Korea, according to US blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis.

North Korea routinely denies involvement in cryptocurrency thefts, and its mission in Geneva did not respond to requests for comment.

Hack involves social engineering, money laundering

While much remains unclear, social engineering, a common tactic in which hackers trick victims into revealing sensitive information or granting access to systems, may have been involved in compromising the laptop, security experts said.

Harry Donnelly, CEO of Circuit, a crypto risk infrastructure company, said companies are planning more employee training to guard against social engineering attacks.

In such attacks, hackers race to launder the funds before the exchange detects the breach and token issuers freeze assets.

Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn linked to Binance, while Circle said it froze $800 million. Bitcoin and ether cannot be frozen because no single entity controls the coins.

Chainalysis said the hackers appeared to be using sophisticated laundering patterns it had not seen before.

On Friday, some crypto exchange executives called for the industry to develop a coordinated hack detection system.

“We need a real-time alert system that allows participants to share information immediately when a hack occurs, coordinate a rapid response, and temporarily freeze suspected stolen funds,” said Star Xu, CEO of crypto exchange OKX, in a post on X.

GSR’s Riezman added that the Binance hack could spur the industry to act: “As we’re at this kind of confluence moment for traditional finance and digital assets, I think it’s obviously important that we continue to improve, and I think this, if anything, will be a catalyst for that.”

headline: Capt Safdar's remarks about women suffering from illness draw criticism, including from CM Maryam
description: "Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible,” the Punjab chief minister says; top lawyers’ bodies condemn remarks about Asma Jahangir.
author: Zulqernain Tahir
article_text:
LAHORE: Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz’s spouse, retired Capt Muhammad Safdar, has come under fire for disparaging remarks about women advocating for bodily autonomy.

Speaking at a Khatm-i-Nabuwwat rally in Chiniot earlier this week, Safdar took aim at the slogan “mera jism, meri marzi” (my body, my choice).

He questioned why women who assert control over their bodies turn to religious scholars for prayers when diagnosed with serious illnesses such as cancer.

“They say, ‘My body, my choice.’ But when they fall ill or develop cancer, they turn to religious scholars, seeking prayers and blessed water for a cure. They should understand that if they claim ownership over their bodies, they should also be able to cure them. In reality, the human body is under God’s control,” he said.

On Friday, Maryam responded to a post on X regarding the speech, which stated: “Maryam Nawaz’s husband, Captain Safdar, also lost his mother-in-law to cancer, yet here he is mocking women who are battling cancer.”

The chief minister’s mother, Kulsoom Nawaz, passed away in 2018 after a months-long battle with cancer.

“Heartbreaking,” the chief minister said, posting an emoji of a broken heart.

“The silent battles a woman, a wife, fights behind closed doors … The strength she must find even when she feels like breaking. Some battles are fought in silence and some wounds are invisible,” she said.

Apart from CM Maryam, users on social media also took issue with Safdar’s remarks.

“My [mother] has been a cancer patient, and God knows how we managed to get through those difficult times. Her survival was nothing short of a miracle. Listening to Capt Safdar’s remarks on this matter is utterly shameful and disgraceful!” said TV anchor Ajmal Jami on X.

He also thanked CM Maryam for her “thoughtful and compassionate words for all those brave women”.

Another user, Maheen Ghani, said: “So a woman who says ‘mera jism, meri marzi’, which is essentially about autonomy and consent, loses the right to ask for prayers when she gets cancer? Is that seriously the argument?

“To take a woman’s illness, her fear and her faith and turn them into an opportunity to humiliate her. What an ugly, twisted understanding of both women’s rights and religion.”

On the other hand, some, like journalist Benazir Shah, lauded CM Maryam for speaking out.

“It takes real courage to take a public stand like this. More power to you, Maryam Nawaz Sharif,” she said.

Lawyers’ bodies condemn remarks about Asma Jahangir

Meanwhile, two premier lawyers’ bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018. During the rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer “cursed”.

Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements.

Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action.

“The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation,” the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly “deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect”.

The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance.

“The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition,” he emphasised.

Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar.

“These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community,” the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination.

“Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination.”

The SCBA also strongly condemned derogatory remarks by Safdar against women and an illness that was “being valiantly fought back by hundreds of thousands of women across the world”.

“At a time when women are breaking barriers, such remarks are disgraceful and entirely unacceptable,” the SCBA said.

“What makes this conduct even more shameful is that his own spouse holds the highest office of Punjab chief minister, and he himself is the father of a daughter; he should have been ashamed of making such insensitive and degrading remarks directed against the women,” it said.

These statements may also attract penal consequences, the SCBA reminded and called upon the concerned authorities to take immediate and strict notice and proceed in accordance with the law.

“Such divisive, offensive, and intolerant attitudes must be firmly challenged and nipped in the bud.

“Let it be clear to all and sundry, we will not remain silent when the dignity of our legal fraternity, the legacy of a human rights champion, and the respect owed to women are attacked,” the SCBA statement said.

Nasir Iqbal from Islamabad also contributed to this report.

“To take a woman’s illness, her fear and her faith and turn them into an opportunity to humiliate her. What an ugly, twisted understanding of both women’s rights and religion.”

On the other hand, some, like journalist Benazir Shah, lauded CM Maryam for speaking out.

“It takes real courage to take a public stand like this. More power to you, Maryam Nawaz Sharif,” she said.

Meanwhile, two premier lawyers’ bodies on Saturday strongly condemned Safdar for his remarks about Asma Jahangir – a renowned senior lawyer and human rights activist who passed away in 2018. During the rally, Safdar had called the late lawyer “cursed”.

Pakistan Bar Council (PBC) Vice Chairman Pir Muhammad Masood Chishti, as well as the 28th executive committee of the outgoing Supreme Court Bar Association (SCBA), regretted the remarks and urged public representatives to exercise restraint and uphold dignity in their statements.

Chishti called upon the relevant authorities to take immediate notice and initiate appropriate legal action.

“The use of disparaging language and references to her religious identity to malign her is highly regrettable and deserves strong condemnation,” the PBC vice chairman regretted, adding that making such remarks against a deceased woman, who was no longer alive to defend herself or respond, was particularly “deplorable and reflects a lack of decency and respect”.

The PBC vice chairman observed that differences of opinion must never become a pretext for personal attacks, hate speech, character assassination or religious intolerance.

“The invaluable services and contributions of the late Asma Jahangir to the legal fraternity, human rights and the rule of law deserve respect and recognition,” he emphasised.

Likewise, the 28th executive committee of the SCBA strongly and unanimously took exception to the recent remarks by Safdar.

“These remarks are highly condemnable and have deeply wounded the sentiments of the entire legal community,” the SCBA said, adding that Jahangir was a devout Muslim who dedicated her life to justice, humanity, and the rights of all people, without discrimination.

“Her services to humanity and human rights transcended religious boundaries and to make such hateful remarks about her was not only deeply disrespectful but also an insult to all those who continue to honour her legacy. She stood for the rights of every individual without discrimination.”

The SCBA also strongly condemned derogatory remarks by Safdar against women and an illness that was “being valiantly fought back by hundreds of thousands of women across the world”.

“At a time when women are breaking barriers, such remarks are disgraceful and entirely unacceptable,” the SCBA said.

“What makes this conduct even more shameful is that his own spouse holds the highest office of Punjab chief minister, and he himself is the father of a daughter; he should have been ashamed of making such insensitive and degrading remarks directed against the women,” it said.

These statements may also attract penal consequences, the SCBA reminded and called upon the concerned authorities to take immediate and strict notice and proceed in accordance with the law.

“Such divisive, offensive, and intolerant attitudes must be firmly challenged and nipped in the bud.

“Let it be clear to all and sundry, we will not remain silent when the dignity of our legal fraternity, the legacy of a human rights champion, and the respect owed to women are attacked,” the SCBA statement said.

Nasir Iqbal from Islamabad also contributed to this report.
